2027-04-04.title: Second Sunday of Resurrection: New Sunday (Puthu Njayar)
2027-04-04.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The nations shall run to you
One heart and soul: the first community
Christ reconciles all things in himself
Thomas the apostle professes his faith
2027-04-04.alt: Second Sunday of Resurrection: New Sunday (Puthu Njayar), the Sunday of the Neophytes, the eighth day of Easter. The calendar notes the fuller passages: Acts 4:32–5:11, Colossians 1:1–20 and John 20:19–31. In the Latin Church this Sunday is also kept as Divine Mercy Sunday, and many Syro-Malabar parishes pray the Divine Mercy devotion today; follow your parish. Around this Sunday great crowds of pilgrims climb to the Kurisumudi at Malayattoor.
2027-04-04.verse: Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!” Jesus said to him, “Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.”
theo: Every Christian in Kerala knows this Sunday by its name: Puthu Njayar, New Sunday. It is the eighth day of Easter, and the Church calls it new because everything has become new: “So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: everything old has passed away; see, everything has become new!” (2 Corinthians 5:17). In the ancient Church the newly baptised, who had worn white all through Easter week, laid aside their white garments on this day and took their place among the faithful; so the Syro-Malabar calendar also calls it the Sunday of the Neophytes. But for the St Thomas Christians it is above all the Sunday of their father in faith. The Gospel of the day is the Gospel of Mar Thoma, and the Church that by tradition he founded on the Malabar coast hears it as a family story. From early morning, and on the days around it, pilgrims climb the rocky hill of Malayattoor, where the tradition of the place holds that the apostle prayed, many of them carrying wooden crosses and calling on him as they climb. The climb is a confession in the body: we come to the hill of Thomas to say with him what he said in the upper room.

The Gospel begins on the evening of Easter day. “When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors of the house where the disciples had met were locked for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them and said, ‘Peace be with you.’” John's phrase ‘the Jews’ here means certain religious authorities of that time; the disciples behind the locked doors were themselves Jews, and the Church warns against reading such words as blame on the Jewish people as a whole (Catechism 597; Nostra Aetate 4). Locked doors do not keep out the Risen Lord. His first word is peace, and his first gesture is to show his wounds: “After he said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Then the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord.” He has risen in the same body that was crucified; the wounds are not erased but glorified, signs of a love stronger than death. Then he sends them: “As the Father has sent me, so I send you.” And he breathes on them, as God breathed into Adam in the beginning (Genesis 2:7): “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained.” On the very evening of the Resurrection the Lord gives his Church the power to forgive sins in his name. The Council of Trent saw in these words the institution of the Sacrament of Penance. The first gift of the Risen Christ is mercy: peace, wounds, the Spirit, forgiveness. That is why many keep this day as the Sunday of Divine Mercy: the mercy of God flows from the wounds of the Risen One.

Thomas was not there. When the others say, “We have seen the Lord,” he answers with the most honest sentence in the Gospel: “Unless I see the mark of the nails in his hands, and put my finger in the mark of the nails and my hand in his side, I will not believe.” This is the same Thomas who had said, when Jesus went up to Bethany, “Let us also go, that we may die with him” (John 11:16), and who had asked at the Last Supper, “Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?” (John 14:5). He is brave, practical, and unwilling to pretend. “A week later his disciples were again in the house, and Thomas was with them.” Note that he stays with the community; his doubt does not take him away from the Church, and it is in the Church, on the eighth day, that the Lord finds him. Jesus speaks to him in his own words: “Put your finger here and see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it in my side. Do not doubt but believe.” And Thomas makes the greatest confession of faith in all the Gospels: “My Lord and my God!” He saw a man; he confessed God. Then Jesus looks beyond Thomas to us: “Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.” In many Kerala churches, when the priest lifts up the consecrated Host and the Chalice, people whisper Thomas's words: My Lord and my God. We do not see the wounds, but we believe that the Risen Lord himself is present, truly and substantially, Body and Blood, soul and divinity. John tells us why he wrote: “so that you may come to believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and that through believing you may have life in his name” (John 20:31).

The other readings show what the faith of Thomas builds. Isaiah sees nations streaming to God: “See, you shall call nations that you do not know, and nations that do not know you shall run to you.” A Church in India, far from Jerusalem, is one of those nations that ran. Isaiah also promises that God's word does not fail: “so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose.” The word that came to the Malabar coast has not returned empty in nearly two thousand years. In Acts we see the fruit of the Resurrection in a community: “Now the whole group of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one claimed private ownership of any possessions, but everything they owned was held in common. With great power the apostles gave their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all. There was not a needy person among them.” Barnabas, “son of encouragement”, sells a field and lays the money at the apostles' feet. Kerala Christian homes once kept the custom of the pidiyari, a handful of rice set aside at every cooking for the Church and the poor: small, daily, and together enough to feed a parish. And Paul sings of the Christ whom Thomas touched: “He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation.” “He is the head of the body, the church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead.” Through him God was pleased “to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, by making peace through the blood of his cross.” The wounds Thomas touched are the wounds through which the whole universe is reconciled to God.
conn: The breath of new creation.

“the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life” (Genesis 2:7); Ezekiel prophesies to the breath over the dry bones (Ezekiel 37:9); the Risen Lord breathes on the disciples (John 20:22).
The wounds.
“he was wounded for our transgressions” (Isaiah 53:5); “when they look on the one whom they have pierced” (Zechariah 12:10); “Look at my hands and my feet; see that it is I myself” (Luke 24:39).
The power to forgive.

Jesus gives Peter the keys of the kingdom (Matthew 16:19); “whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven” (Matthew 18:18); on Easter evening, “If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them” (John 20:23).
Thomas the Twin.

“Let us also go, that we may die with him” (John 11:16); “How can we know the way?” and the answer, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:5–6); Thomas fishes with Peter when the Risen Lord appears by the lake (John 21:2).
Blessed without seeing.

“Blessed is she who believed” (Luke 1:45); “Although you have not seen him, you love him” (1 Peter 1:8); “faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1).
One heart and soul.

The first community devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and the prayers (Acts 2:42); “How very good and pleasant it is when kindred live together in unity!” (Psalm 133:1); Christ “became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9).
The firstborn from the dead.
Christ is “the firstborn from the dead” (Colossians 1:18) and “the first fruits of those who have died” (1 Corinthians 15:20); “I was dead, and see, I am alive forever and ever” (Revelation 1:18).
altar: “A week later his disciples were again in the house.” From the first Easter the disciples gathered on the eighth day, and the Lord came to them. Every Sunday Qurbana is that upper room: the doors of our fears are closed, and the Risen Lord comes and stands among us and says, Peace be with you.

When the priest raises the Body and Blood of the Lord, many Syro-Malabar faithful whisper the words of Mar Thoma: My Lord and my God. We do not see the wounds as Thomas did, but we believe that the Lord who is lifted up before us is truly present, the same Lord who rose from the tomb.

The Lord who breathed the Spirit for the forgiveness of sins still forgives through the priest in the Sacrament of Reconciliation. New Sunday is a good day to come back to confession and so to approach the altar with a heart made new.
outline: Opening
A long line of pilgrims climbing the rock of Malayattoor in the dark.
Point 1 · Peace be with you
Locked doors, shown wounds and the joy of the disciples.
Point 2 · Receive the Holy Spirit
The breath of new creation and the power to forgive sins.
Point 3 · My Lord and my God
The doubt of Thomas, the wounds touched, the greatest confession.
Point 4 · One heart and soul
The community born of the Resurrection: the nations run, the poor are fed.
Closing image
A grandmother whispering at the elevation: My Lord and my God.
Take-home line
“Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.”
live: Whisper the confession (John 20:28)
At every Holy Qurbana this season, when the Host and Chalice are raised, say in your heart: My Lord and my God.
Come back to confession (John 20:23)
If it has been a long time, go to the Sacrament of Reconciliation in this Easter season; the Risen Lord instituted it on Easter night.
Keep the pidiyari (Acts 4:34)
Revive the old custom in a new way: set aside a small amount daily this season for the poor or for your parish.
Stay with the community (John 20:26)
If you or someone you love is struggling with doubt, do not leave the Sunday assembly; invite them to come with you next Sunday.
Pray for the St Thomas Christians
Pray today for the Syro-Malabar Church in Kerala and in every land of migration, that it may keep the faith of Mar Thoma.
fathers: St Gregory the Great (in substance)

It was not by chance that Thomas was absent and then came, heard, doubted, touched and believed. The unbelief of Thomas has done more for our faith than the faith of the disciples who believed at once. While he is brought back to faith by touching, our minds are freed from doubt and made firm in faith. The disciple who doubted and touched the wounds became a witness to the reality of the Resurrection.
St Augustine (in substance)

Thomas saw and touched the man, and confessed the God whom he neither saw nor touched. Through what he saw he believed what he did not see. And the Lord calls us blessed, who have not seen and yet believe, for we are the ones of whom he spoke.
St Cyril of Alexandria (in substance)

As in the beginning God breathed the breath of life into the man he had formed, so now Christ, renewing his creation, breathes the Holy Spirit upon his disciples. The first breath made Adam a living being; the second makes us a new creation, sharers in the divine nature.
magis: Catechism 644
Even when faced with the reality of the Risen Jesus the disciples were still doubting; Christ's Resurrection was not the product of their credulity.
Catechism 645
The Risen Jesus invites the disciples to touch him, establishing that he is not a ghost; his body is real, the same body that was tortured and crucified, but glorified.
Catechism 448
Thomas's confession ‘My Lord and my God!’ confesses the divinity of Jesus.
Catechism 976 and 1485
On Easter evening the Lord gave his apostles the Holy Spirit and the power to forgive sins; this power is exercised in the Sacrament of Penance.
Catechism 952
In the first community everything was held in common; the Christian is a steward of the Lord's goods for the sake of the neighbour and the poor.
Catechism 1166–1167
Sunday, the eighth day, is the day of the Resurrection, when the faithful gather to hear the word and take part in the Eucharist.
saints: Today
4 April: New Sunday (Puthu Njayar), the confession of St Thomas the Apostle, father in faith of the St Thomas Christians. In the Latin Church this Sunday is also Divine Mercy Sunday.
2027-04-04.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you came through locked doors and stood among your frightened disciples, saying, Peace be with you. You showed them your hands and your side, you breathed on them the Holy Spirit, and you gave your Church the power to forgive sins. You did not abandon Thomas in his doubt, but came back for him on the eighth day and let him touch your wounds. With Mar Thoma, our father in faith, we confess you: My Lord and my God! Make us blessed among those who have not seen and yet believe. Make our parishes one heart and soul, with no one in need among us, and send us to the nations as the Father sent you. Through the prayers of your holy Mother, who believed without seeing, keep the Church of Mar Thoma faithful in every land. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-04-11.title: Third Sunday of Resurrection
2027-04-11.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The Lord gives salvation to all who keep his covenant
Redemption through the blood of Christ
Jesus, the Way to the Father
2027-04-11.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The third Sunday of the season of the Resurrection. In this season the Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of the Apostles Mar Addai and Mar Mari. The Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost. Pilgrims continue to climb the hill of Malayattoor, the shrine of Saint Thomas, in the weeks after New Sunday (times as the shrine announces).
2027-04-11.verse: Jesus said to him, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.”
theo: On this third Sunday of the Resurrection the Church opens with a prophecy about who belongs in God's house. Isaiah speaks to two kinds of people who expected to be shut out. The foreigner thought, “The LORD will surely separate me from his people”; the eunuch, who could have no children to carry on his name, said, “I am just a dry tree.” God answers both with a promise beyond their hopes. To the eunuchs who keep his covenant he says, “I will give, in my house and within my walls, a monument and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that shall not be cut off.” And to the foreigners who love his name he says, “these I will bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer… for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.” Jesus quoted this verse when he cleansed the temple (Mark 11:17). After Easter the promise comes true in a way no one could have imagined: in the Acts of the Apostles one of the very first to be baptised from beyond Israel is an Ethiopian eunuch, who was reading Isaiah in his chariot when Philip found him (Acts 8:26–39). The Risen Lord gathers the outcasts. In his Church no one is a dry tree, and no nation is a stranger. We Indians, whom the Gospel reached through the Apostle Thomas, are ourselves the foreigners whom God brought to his holy mountain.

The second reading takes us into the council in Jerusalem, where the apostles have been arrested again for preaching the name of Jesus. Some want to put them to death. Then a remarkable man stands up: “a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law, respected by all the people.” He was the teacher at whose feet Saul of Tarsus had studied (Acts 22:3). Gamaliel reminds the council of other movements that rose and vanished, and gives advice of real wisdom: “keep away from these men and let them alone; because if this plan or this undertaking is of human origin, it will fail; but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them.” The Church remembers Gamaliel with honour: a devout Jewish teacher whose fear of God made him just. His words have been proved by two thousand years of history: empires that tried to destroy the Church have fallen, and the Church remains, not because of her own strength but because her work is of God. The apostles are flogged and released, and Luke records their response: “As they left the council, they rejoiced that they were considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the sake of the name. And every day in the temple and at home they did not cease to teach and proclaim Jesus as the Messiah.” In the temple and at home: the faith was handed on in public worship and around family tables, as it has been in Kerala for centuries.

Paul's letter to the Ephesians begins with one long hymn of blessing, in the form of the great Jewish prayers of praise: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places.” In one breathless sentence Paul unfolds the whole plan of God. We were chosen in Christ “before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless before him in love.” We were destined “for adoption as his children through Jesus Christ.” “In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace that he lavished on us.” God's purpose is “to gather up all things in him, things in heaven and things on earth.” And then Paul speaks to us directly: “In him you also, when you had heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and had believed in him, were marked with the seal of the promised Holy Spirit; this is the pledge of our inheritance.” The seal is the mark of ownership; the pledge is the first instalment, the advance that guarantees the full payment. The Holy Spirit given in Baptism and Chrismation is heaven already begun in us. The great prayer of thanksgiving in the Holy Qurbana, the Anaphora of Mar Addai and Mar Mari, one of the most ancient Eucharistic prayers in the world, sings this same blessing: praise to the Father who has done all this for us through his Son and in the Holy Spirit.

The Gospel brings us to the Last Supper, where Jesus speaks to frightened disciples: “Do not let your hearts be troubled. Believe in God, believe also in me. In my Father's house there are many dwelling places… I go to prepare a place for you.” Then Saint Thomas asks the question that every honest disciple has asked: “Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?” We Saint Thomas Christians should love this question. Our father in faith did not pretend to understand; he asked. And because he asked, we received one of the greatest sentences in the Gospel: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.” Jesus does not give Thomas a map; he gives himself. The way to the Father is not a road we must find but a Person we must follow. The same Thomas who said ‘we do not know the way’ would one day kneel before the Risen Lord and say, “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28), and would walk the way to India and lay down his life there. Then Philip asks, “Lord, show us the Father, and we will be satisfied,” and Jesus answers, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” In the face of Jesus, the human face of God, we see who the Father is. And he promises that those who believe will do “greater works than these,” and that whatever we ask in his name he will do. Every Holy Qurbana ends with that promise: we have been fed by the Way, taught by the Truth, filled with the Life; now we go out on the road, asking in his name.
conn: A house of prayer for all.

“For my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples” (Isaiah 56:7); Jesus quotes it in the temple (Mark 11:17); “you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are citizens with the saints and also members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19).
The eunuch who believed.
Philip, beginning with the scripture from Isaiah, proclaims the good news about Jesus to the Ethiopian eunuch, and baptises him (Acts 8:35–38).
Gamaliel's pupil.
Paul says, “I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel” (Acts 22:3).
Unless the Lord builds.
“Unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Psalm 127:1).
Chosen and blessed.
God says to Abraham, “I will bless you, and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing” (Genesis 12:2); in Christ we are blessed “with every spiritual blessing” (Ephesians 1:3).
Sealed with the Spirit.

“Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, with which you were marked with a seal for the day of redemption” (Ephesians 4:30); God anoints us “by putting his seal on us and giving us his Spirit in our hearts as a first installment” (2 Corinthians 1:22).
The way.
“You show me the path of life” (Psalm 16:11); Jesus opened for us “the new and living way… through his flesh” (Hebrews 10:20); the first Christians were called followers of “the Way” (Acts 9:2).
Thomas the apostle.
Thomas says, “Let us also go, that we may die with him” (John 11:16), and confesses the Risen Lord, “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana, in the Anaphora of Mar Addai and Mar Mari, the Church blesses the Father for every spiritual blessing given in Christ, and the redemption won by his blood becomes present on the altar. Christ, the Way, the Truth and the Life, is truly present and gives himself to us.
Each Holy Communion is the pledge of our inheritance: the Lord who has gone to prepare a place for us comes to us now, so that where he is we may be also.
The house of prayer for all peoples is gathered around the one altar: foreigners and outcasts, sinners and saints, all made one family in the Body of Christ.
outline: Opening
Who belongs in God's house?
Point 1 · A house of prayer for all peoples
The foreigner and the eunuch gathered in.
Point 2 · If it is of God
Gamaliel's wisdom and the apostles' joy.
Point 3 · Every spiritual blessing
Chosen, adopted, redeemed and sealed.
Point 4 · I am the way
Thomas's question and the Lord's answer.
Closing image
Pilgrims climbing the hill of Malayattoor, following the crosses in the dark.
Take-home line
“I am the way, and the truth, and the life.”
live: Welcome the outsider (Isaiah 56:7)
Make a newcomer, a migrant worker or a lonely person welcome at church this week: greet them, sit with them, invite them home.
Trust God's work (Acts 5:39)
Bring one worry about the Church or your family to prayer, and leave it with God whose work cannot be overthrown.
Bless the Father (Ephesians 1:3)
Each morning this week, before anything else, say: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Ask Thomas's question (John 14:5)
Bring one honest question about faith to the Lord in prayer, or to a priest or catechist, as Thomas did.
Pray in his name (John 14:13)
Write down one intention and pray for it daily this week in the name of Jesus.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

Christ is the way by which we go and the home to which we go. As man he is the way; as God he is the goal. Go by him who is man, and you will arrive at him who is God. Do not look for any other way to him than himself.
St Irenaeus of Lyons (in substance)

The Son is the visible of the Father, and the Father is the invisible of the Son. Whoever sees the Son sees the Father, because the Father has made himself known in the Son. And the glory of God is a human being fully alive, and the life of a human being is the vision of God.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Gamaliel spoke more truly than he knew. If the preaching of the apostles had been of men, it would have perished with them; but fishermen, flogged and imprisoned, conquered the world. This is the proof that the work was of God.
magis: Catechism 2664
There is no other way of Christian prayer than Christ; our prayer has access to the Father only if we pray in the name of Jesus.
Catechism 516
Christ's whole earthly life, his words and deeds, his silences and sufferings, is the revelation of the Father: whoever has seen me has seen the Father.
Catechism 1296
Christ himself declared that he was marked with his Father's seal; Christians too are marked with a seal, the seal of the Holy Spirit, for the day of redemption.
Catechism 1025
To live in heaven is to be with Christ; the elect live in him, and there they find their true identity, their own name.
Catechism 831
The Church is catholic because she has been sent by Christ on a mission to the whole of the human race; all are called to belong to the new People of God.
saints: This week

Sunday 11 April: the Third Sunday of Resurrection. Monday 12 to Saturday 17 April: the third week of the Resurrection. Sunday 18 April: the Fourth Sunday of Resurrection, the World Day of Prayer for Vocations.
2027-04-11.prayer: Blessed are you, God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who have blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing. You chose us before the foundation of the world, adopted us as your children, redeemed us through the blood of your Son, and sealed us with the promised Holy Spirit. Make your Church a house of prayer for all peoples, where no one is a stranger. Give us the wisdom of Gamaliel to recognise your work and the joy of the apostles to suffer for the name of Jesus. Lord Jesus, our Way, our Truth and our Life, as you answered the question of our father Saint Thomas, lead us to the Father, and bring us to the place you have prepared for us. With the Father and the Holy Spirit, to you be glory for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-04-18.title: Fourth Sunday of Resurrection · World Prayer Day for Vocations
2027-04-18.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: God will never forget his people
God's gift cannot be bought with money
Salvation is the gift of God
Your pain will turn into joy
2027-04-18.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). Fourth Sunday of the Resurrection, kept as the World Prayer Day for Vocations. The calendar notes the fuller passages: Ephesians 1:15–2:7 and John 16:16–33. “Queen of Heaven” is prayed until Pentecost.
2027-04-18.verse: So you have pain now; but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.
theo: The first reading was spoken to a people in exile, far from a ruined Jerusalem. The prophet begins with a burst of praise: “Sing for joy, O heavens, and exult, O earth; break forth, O mountains, into singing! For the LORD has comforted his people, and will have compassion on his suffering ones.” But Zion does not feel comforted. She says what many of us have said in the dark: “The LORD has forsaken me, my Lord has forgotten me.” God answers with one of the tenderest sentences in the Bible: “Can a woman forget her nursing child, or show no compassion for the child of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you. See, I have inscribed you on the palms of my hands.” A mother's love is the strongest human love we know, and God says his love is stronger still. In the Easter season the image of the palms takes on new meaning. On the evening of the Resurrection the Risen Lord “showed them his hands and his side” (John 20:20), and to Thomas he said, “Put your finger here and see my hands” (John 20:27). Our names are written in those wounded hands. Then Isaiah describes a reversal no one could imagine. Zion, who thought herself “bereaved and barren, exiled and put away”, suddenly finds her house too small: “The place is too crowded for me; make room for me to settle.” She asks in wonder, “Who has borne me these?” This is the fruitfulness of the Church, the mother who receives children from every nation. On this World Prayer Day for Vocations we remember that every priest, every religious sister and brother, every missionary is a child the Lord has given to his Church. Kerala has given many such children to the whole world, and today, when fewer young people answer, Isaiah's promise holds: “those who wait for me shall not be put to shame.”

In Acts, the deacon Philip has preached Christ in Samaria, and “there was great joy in that city” (Acts 8:8). The apostles in Jerusalem send Peter and John. “The two went down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit (for as yet the Spirit had not come upon any of them; they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus). Then Peter and John laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.” The Church has always seen here the gift of the Spirit that completes the grace of Baptism; in the Eastern tradition the anointing with holy Myron is closely joined to Baptism itself. It also shows the bond between a new community and the apostles: the Samaritans are not left on their own but joined to the one Church through those whom Christ sent. Then a dark figure steps forward. Simon, who had practised magic and been admired as a great power, sees what happens through the laying on of hands and offers money: “Give me also this power so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit.” Peter's answer is fierce: “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain God's gift with money! You have no part or share in this, for your heart is not right before God.” From Simon's name the Church calls the buying or selling of spiritual things simony. The lesson goes deeper than money. A vocation to the priesthood or religious life is not a career to be purchased, a family status to be secured, or a power to be used. It is a gift and a call, received freely and given freely: “You received without payment; give without payment” (Matthew 10:8). Peter still leaves the door open: “Repent therefore of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord,” and Simon asks for prayer. Even here, mercy is not shut out.

Paul tells the Ephesians the truth about where we all began: “You were dead through the trespasses and sins in which you once lived, following the course of this world.” Not weak or confused, but dead, unable to raise ourselves. Then the two most hopeful words of the letter: “But God”. “But God, who is rich in mercy, out of the great love with which he loved us even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ.” Paul interrupts himself to make sure we do not miss the point: “by grace you have been saved”. And he goes further: God “raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus.” The Resurrection is not only something that happened to Jesus on the first Easter; in Baptism it has already begun in us. We are seated with him, so that “in the ages to come he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.” Simon the magician wanted to buy what can only be received. Paul reminds us that the whole of salvation is a gift. Every vocation begins here: not with my plan for my life, but with God's kindness, which made me alive when I was dead.

The Gospel takes us back to the Last Supper. Jesus says, “A little while, and you will no longer see me, and again a little while, and you will see me.” The disciples do not understand: “What does he mean by this ‘a little while’? We do not know what he is talking about.” We understand it now because we live after Easter. The first little while was the time from Thursday night to the tomb; the second little while ended on the morning of the Resurrection. Jesus does not hide the pain: “Very truly, I tell you, you will weep and mourn, but the world will rejoice; you will have pain, but your pain will turn into joy.” He does not say the pain will be replaced by joy, but turned into it, as the labour of a mother becomes the joy of a child. “When a woman is in labor, she has pain, because her hour has come. But when her child is born, she no longer remembers the anguish because of the joy of having brought a human being into the world.” The Fathers saw in these words the Church giving birth to new children through the Cross, and Christian tradition has also thought of the Blessed Virgin Mary standing by the Cross, where her Son gave her to the beloved disciple as his mother (John 19:26–27). Then comes the promise for every disciple: “So you have pain now; but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.” A vocation is not without pain; priests and religious know the labour of their ministry. But it carries a joy that no one can take away, because it is the joy of the Risen Lord. And Jesus adds an invitation: “Ask and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete.” On this day the Church asks, as Jesus told her to ask, that the Lord of the harvest will send labourers into his harvest (Matthew 9:38).
conn: Written on his palms.
“See, I have inscribed you on the palms of my hands” (Isaiah 49:16); the Risen Lord “showed them his hands and his side” (John 20:20) and invited Thomas to see his hands (John 20:27).
Stronger than a mother.
God compares his love to a mother's: “As a mother comforts her child, so I will comfort you” (Isaiah 66:13); Jesus longed to gather Jerusalem's children as a hen gathers her brood (Luke 13:34).
Philip in Samaria.
The deacon Philip, one of the seven chosen in Acts 6:5, proclaimed the Messiah in Samaria (Acts 8:5–8), where Jesus himself had once been welcomed by many Samaritans (John 4:39–42).
The laying on of hands.

The Spirit is given through the laying on of the apostles' hands (Acts 8:17; 19:6); Paul reminds Timothy “to rekindle the gift of God that is within you through the laying on of my hands” (2 Timothy 1:6).
Freely received.
“You received without payment; give without payment” (Matthew 10:8); “by grace you have been saved” (Ephesians 2:5, 8).
Pray for labourers.
“The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest” (Matthew 9:37–38).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Risen Lord shows us his hands once more, in the Bread broken and the Cup offered. The priest who stands at the altar does not own this gift and cannot buy it; he has received it by the laying on of hands, and he gives freely what he freely received.

Every Qurbana is also a school of joy. The sorrow of the Cross becomes the joy of the Resurrection on the altar, and from the altar the Church prays that the Lord may raise up new priests and religious to serve his people.
outline: Opening
A mother who cannot forget her child, and wounded hands with our names written on them.
Point 1 · I will not forget you
God's love stronger than a mother's; a barren Zion crowded with children.
Point 2 · You thought you could buy God's gift
The Spirit given through the apostles; vocations as gift, not career.
Point 3 · But God, rich in mercy
Dead in sin, made alive and seated with Christ.
Point 4 · Your pain will turn into joy
The woman in labour, the Mother at the Cross, and a joy no one can take.
Closing image
A crowded house where a lonely mother once lived, children arriving from every road.
Take-home line
“No one will take your joy from you.”
live: Remember the palms (Isaiah 49:16)
When you feel forgotten this week, look at your own palm and pray: Lord, my name is written on your hands.
Give freely (Acts 8:20)
Examine whether you use anything holy, a church role, a family connection, a donation, to gain honour or advantage, and let it go.
Pray for vocations (Matthew 9:38)
Pray every day this week for a vocation from your own family or parish, and for the priests and religious who serve you.
Ask in his name (John 16:24)
Bring one sorrow to the Lord in prayer every day this week, and ask him to turn it into joy.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

This ‘little while’ is the whole span of the present age, short as it is when we look at it from its end. Now we have sorrow, for we long for the Lord and do not yet see him. But a little while, and we shall see him, and there we shall ask nothing, because nothing will be lacking to us, and no one will take that joy away.
St Cyril of Jerusalem (in substance)

Simon the magician once came to the font. He was baptised, but he was not enlightened. He dipped his body in water but did not open his heart to the Spirit. Do not come to holy things as he did, with a hidden purpose; come with a sincere heart, and the Spirit will be given to you.
magis: Catechism 219
God's love for his people is compared to a father's love for his son and is stronger than a mother's love for her children (Isaiah 49:14–15).
Catechism 1288
From the time of the apostles, by the laying on of hands, the gift of the Spirit that completes the grace of Baptism was imparted to the newly baptised (Acts 8:15–17).
Catechism 2121
Simony is the buying or selling of spiritual things; Peter's answer to Simon the magician shows that God's gift cannot be bought.
Catechism 1578
No one has a right to receive the sacrament of Holy Orders; no one claims this office for himself, but is called to it by God.
Catechism 1996
Our justification comes from the grace of God: the free and undeserved help that God gives us to become his children.
saints: This week

19–24 Apr: the fourth week of the Resurrection. 24 Apr (Saturday): St George, Martyr, an Important Feast in the Syro-Malabar calendar (First Set), and the patron's day of Mar George Alencherry and the other bishops who bear the name George. 25 Apr: Fifth Sunday of the Resurrection, with the memory of Mar Addai (verify locally).
2027-04-18.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you have written our names on the palms of your wounded hands, and you never forget us. Pour out on your Church the Holy Spirit, whom no one can buy, and keep us from treating any holy thing as a possession or a career. Rich in mercy, you made us alive when we were dead and seated us with you in the heavenly places. Turn our sorrows into joy, and give us the joy that no one can take from us. Lord of the harvest, send labourers into your harvest: call from our families and parishes good priests, holy religious and faithful missionaries, and give them generous hearts to answer. With the Blessed Virgin Mary, who stood by your Cross and rejoiced in your Resurrection, we give glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-04-25.title: Fifth Sunday of Resurrection (Mar Addai)
2027-04-25.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The Lord who prepares the meal
2027-04-25.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The calendar keeps Mar Addai, the apostle of Edessa, on the Fifth Sunday of Resurrection, whatever its date (this year 25 April); his name, with that of Mar Mari, is borne by the anaphora most used in our Qurbana. Longer forms in the calendar: Acts 9:1–19; Hebrews 10:19–36. The feast of St Mark the Evangelist (25 April) gives way to the Sunday this year (verify locally).
2027-04-25.verse: Jesus said to them, “Come and have breakfast.” Now none of the disciples dared to ask him, “Who are you?” because they knew it was the Lord.
theo: This Sunday carries the name of Mar Addai. The Church of the East has always honoured Addai and his disciple Mari as the apostles who carried the Gospel to Edessa and to Mesopotamia, and our Syro-Malabar Church, which shares that East Syriac heritage, prays at most of its Qurbanas the Anaphora of the Apostles Mar Addai and Mar Mari, one of the most ancient Eucharistic prayers still in use anywhere in the world. What do we know of Addai? The historian Eusebius, writing in the early fourth century, records a tradition he found in the archives of Edessa: after the Ascension, the apostle Thomas sent Thaddeus, one of the seventy disciples, to King Abgar of Edessa, who was healed and received the faith. The Syriac Teaching of Addai tells the same story with many additions. Historians cannot verify every detail, and we hold them as tradition, but the core is precious: Edessa became one of the first Christian cities, the cradle of Syriac Christianity, and its memory links Addai to Thomas, our own father in faith. In 2001, in guidelines for the Chaldean Church and the Assyrian Church of the East, the Holy See recognised the validity of this ancient anaphora even in the form used by the Assyrian Church of the East, which has no explicit narrative of the Last Supper. When our priest prays it, he prays in the words of a Church that has offered the Sacrifice in the language close to that of Jesus since the first centuries.

The readings of the Fifth Sunday of Resurrection begin with the Servant of the LORD in Isaiah. He is “deeply despised, abhorred by the nations, the slave of rulers”, yet God promises: “Kings shall see and stand up, princes, and they shall prostrate themselves.” God gives the Servant “as a covenant to the people”, to say “to the prisoners, ‘Come out,’ to those who are in darkness, ‘Show yourselves.’” The returning exiles will not hunger or thirst, “for he who has pity on them will lead them, and by springs of water will guide them.” And all creation is invited to sing: “Sing for joy, O heavens, and exult, O earth; break forth, O mountains, into singing! For the LORD has comforted his people, and will have compassion on his suffering ones.” The despised Servant who is exalted is Christ, rejected on Good Friday and raised at Easter. Paul quotes this very chapter when he writes, “See, now is the acceptable time; see, now is the day of salvation!” In the Acts of the Apostles we see the prisoner of darkness called out. Saul, “still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord”, sets out for Damascus with letters to arrest those “who belonged to the Way”. A light from heaven flashes around him, he falls to the ground, and a voice asks: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” “Who are you, Lord?” “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.” The Risen Lord so identifies himself with his Church that to strike the disciples is to strike him. Saul rises blind and is led by the hand into the city; for three days he neither eats nor drinks. The longer reading tells how Ananias, sent by the Lord, lays hands on him: something like scales fall from his eyes, he is baptised, and he eats and is strengthened.

The Letter to the Hebrews draws the conclusion for us who have been baptised: “Therefore, my friends, since we have confidence to enter the sanctuary by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain (that is, through his flesh), and since we have a great priest over the house of God, let us approach with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.” Hearts sprinkled and bodies washed: the writer is thinking of Baptism. The curtain of the Temple that hid the Holy of Holies has been opened in the torn flesh of Christ, and now we may come near. Three exhortations follow: let us approach, let us hold fast to the confession of our hope, and “let us consider how to provoke one another to love and good deeds, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day approaching.” Already in the first century some Christians were staying away from the Sunday assembly. The letter's answer is not a scolding but a reminder: we need one another, and we need the meeting at the altar where the new and living way is opened. Our Qurbana begins with the veil drawn before the sanctuary in some of our churches and opened for the celebration, a living sign of this very text.

The Gospel takes us back to the lakeshore. Seven disciples have gone home to Galilee, Peter, Thomas, Nathanael, the sons of Zebedee and two others, and Peter says, “I am going fishing.” They toil all night and catch nothing. At daybreak a stranger on the beach calls: “Children, you have no fish, have you?” “Cast the net to the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” The net fills so full they cannot haul it in. The beloved disciple is the first to see: “It is the Lord!” Peter, impulsive as ever, throws on his clothes and jumps into the sea. On the shore they find a charcoal fire, fish laid on it, and bread. The Lord who once asked for five loaves now has breakfast ready, and still he says, “Bring some of the fish that you have just caught.” He wants our work joined to his gift. Then the gentle invitation: “Come and have breakfast.” No one dares to ask, “Who are you?” because they know it is the Lord. “Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and did the same with the fish.” It is the third time he has shown himself to them after rising from the dead, and again he makes himself known at a meal. Among the seven is Thomas, the apostle who would carry the Gospel east and, by our tradition, to the shores of Kerala, and who, Eusebius tells us, sent Thaddeus, the Addai of Syriac tradition, to Edessa. A Church of fishermen, sent from a lakeshore breakfast to the ends of the earth: this is our story too. Every Sunday the Risen Lord stands on the shore of our tired week, calls us children, fills our empty nets with his grace, and says at the altar, Come and eat.
conn: The day of salvation.
Paul quotes Isaiah 49:8: “At an acceptable time I have listened to you, and on a day of salvation I have helped you” (2 Corinthians 6:2).
Prisoners, come out.
Jesus reads in Nazareth: “He has sent me to proclaim release to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind” (Luke 4:18); Saul is released from blindness.
Why do you persecute me?

Jesus says, “just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40); Paul later calls himself “the least of the apostles” because he persecuted the Church (1 Corinthians 15:9).
The torn curtain.
At the death of Jesus “the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom” (Mark 15:38); now we enter “through the curtain (that is, through his flesh)” (Hebrews 10:20).
Not neglecting to meet together.
The first believers “devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers” (Acts 2:42).
Fishers of people.
At the first call by the same lake Jesus said, “Follow me, and I will make you fish for people” (Matthew 4:19); the full net recalls the miraculous catch of Luke 5:4–11.
You prepare a table.
“You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies” (Psalm 23:5); the Lord prepares the breakfast on the shore.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana, prayed in the Anaphora of Mar Addai and Mar Mari, the Risen Lord does what he did at the lakeshore: he takes the bread and gives it to us. We bring the fish we have caught, our work and our offerings, and he joins them to his own gift.
Hebrews calls us to approach with a true heart through the new and living way of his flesh: the opened sanctuary of our churches is the sign that in the Qurbana heaven is opened to us.
outline: Opening
Mar Addai, Edessa, and the oldest words of our Qurbana.
Point 1 · Sing for joy, O heavens
The despised Servant exalted, and the prisoners called out.
Point 2 · Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?
The Risen Lord one with his Church.
Point 3 · Let us approach with a true heart
The new and living way, and the Sunday assembly.
Point 4 · Come and have breakfast
The empty night, the full net and the Lord on the shore.
Closing image
Fishing boats returning to Neendakara at dawn, and a family walking to the Sunday Qurbana.
Take-home line
“It is the Lord!”
live: Never skip the Sunday assembly (Hebrews 10:25)
Bring someone who has been away from the Sunday Qurbana with you next week.
See Christ in the persecuted (Acts 9:4)
Pray this week for those who persecute Christians, as the Church prayed for Saul.
Bring your catch (John 21:10)
Offer your week's work at the Qurbana: name it silently at the offertory.
Learn the anaphora
Read slowly one prayer of the Anaphora of Mar Addai and Mar Mari this week and thank God for our apostolic heritage.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

The fish laid on the fire is Christ who suffered; the bread is Christ who came down from heaven. To this meal the Lord invites those whom he finds toiling, and he adds to it the fish they caught, so that the Church may know that her labour is joined to his Passion and made fruitful by it.
St Jerome (in substance)

Those who study the nature of fish say there are a hundred and fifty-three kinds; so the net of the Gospel draws in every kind of people, and the net is not torn. The one Church holds them all, and none is lost.
magis: Catechism 645
The Risen Jesus establishes direct contact with his disciples through touch and the sharing of a meal; he invites them to recognise that he is not a ghost.
Catechism 1329
The Eucharist is called the Breaking of Bread, because Jesus used this rite as head of the table, and the disciples recognised him by this action after his Resurrection.
Catechism 442
Paul's conversion on the road to Damascus: God was pleased to reveal his Son to him so that he might proclaim him among the Gentiles.
Catechism 2178
The practice of the Christian assembly dates from the beginnings of the apostolic age; the Letter to the Hebrews reminds the faithful not to neglect to meet together.
Catechism 1203
The liturgical traditions or rites presently in use in the Church include the Chaldean (East Syriac) tradition; all lawfully recognised rites are of equal right and dignity.
saints: Today

Fifth Sunday of Resurrection, with Mar Addai, apostle of Edessa. In the Latin calendar the Fifth Sunday of Easter; the feast of St Mark the Evangelist is not kept this year because it falls on a Sunday of Easter.
Next week
26–30 April: fifth week of the Resurrection. Thu 29: St Catherine of Siena.
2027-04-25.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you stood on the shore at daybreak, filled the empty nets of your disciples and fed them with bread and fish. You called Saul out of darkness and made the persecutor an apostle. Through the prayers of Mar Addai and Mar Mari, and of Mar Thoma our father in faith, keep our Church faithful to the faith of the apostles. Give us confidence to approach you with a true heart, make us faithful to the Sunday assembly, and let us recognise you each time you say to us at the altar, Come and eat. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-04-01.title: First Thursday of Resurrection
2027-04-01.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The election of the seven deacons
Jesus sends out his twelve disciples
2027-04-01.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The first week of the Resurrection, the week of the newly baptised. The calendar notes the fuller passages: Isaiah 54:1–15 and Colossians 2:8–3:4. Since the Monday after Hosanna Sunday the Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Mar Addai and Mar Mari.
2027-04-01.verse: Cure the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons. You received without payment; give without payment.
theo: Five days after Easter the Church hears a song addressed to a woman who has no children. “Sing, O barren one who did not bear; burst into song and shout, you who have not been in labor! For the children of the desolate woman will be more than the children of her that is married, says the LORD.” Isaiah was speaking to Jerusalem in exile, a city that looked finished, a mother with an empty house. And God tells her to start building extensions: “Enlarge the site of your tent, and let the curtains of your habitations be stretched out; do not hold back; lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes.” Children are coming whom she never expected. Paul reads this song as a word about the Church (Galatians 4:26–27), and the Easter liturgy reads it this week for a reason. On the night of the Resurrection the font gave birth to new sons and daughters; the Church that seemed so small on Good Friday, a handful of women and one disciple at the Cross, now has to widen her tent. The heart of the passage is the tenderness of God: “For a brief moment I abandoned you, but with great compassion I will gather you.” And he binds himself with the oath he swore to Noah: “For the mountains may depart and the hills be removed, but my steadfast love shall not depart from you, and my covenant of peace shall not be removed, says the LORD, who has compassion on you.” Whatever moment of abandonment we have passed through, Easter says it was a brief moment. The steadfast love remains.

The tent grows, and growth brings trouble. In Acts the community in Jerusalem has become large and mixed: Greek-speaking believers and Aramaic-speaking believers, all of them Jews who believe in Jesus. “The Hellenists complained against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution of food.” The apostles do not deny the problem or tell the complainers to be quiet. They gather the whole community and make a decision that will shape the Church for ever. “It is not right that we should neglect the word of God in order to wait on tables. Therefore, friends, select from among yourselves seven men of good standing, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we may appoint to this task, while we, for our part, will devote ourselves to prayer and to serving the word.” The seven are chosen, all with Greek names, from the very group that felt neglected; the apostles pray and lay hands on them. The Church has always seen here the beginning of the diaconate. And the result? “The word of God continued to spread; the number of the disciples increased greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith.” Care for widows and the preaching of the word are not rivals; when the poor are served, the word runs faster. Paul tells the Colossians where this new life comes from: “when you were buried with him in baptism, you were also raised with him through faith in the power of God, who raised him from the dead.” God has cancelled our debt, “erasing the record that stood against us with its legal demands. He set this aside, nailing it to the cross.” On the Cross Christ “disarmed the rulers and authorities and made a public example of them, triumphing over them in it.” The newly baptised do not have to fight their old masters in their own strength. The battle has already been won.

The Gospel takes us back to the beginning of the mission. “Then Jesus summoned his twelve disciples and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to cure every disease and every sickness.” Matthew lists them by name, and among them, in the pair “Thomas and Matthew the tax collector”, is the apostle whom the Christians of Kerala call their father in faith. Jesus gives them a message and a manner. The message: “As you go, proclaim the good news, ‘The kingdom of heaven has come near.’” The manner: “You received without payment; give without payment.” They are to travel without gold, without a bag, without a spare tunic, depending on the welcome of those who receive them. They bring peace into houses: “As you enter the house, greet it. If the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it.” Read in Easter week, this Gospel reminds us that the mission did not begin after the Resurrection; it was rehearsed in Galilee, and the Risen Lord now gives it its full meaning. What the apostles received without payment was, in the end, life from the dead. Every Christian has received the same: forgiveness, Baptism, the Body and Blood of the Lord, none of it earned. So everything we give, our time to a lonely widow, our money to the poor, our word of faith to a doubting friend, is only the overflow of what was given to us without payment. A Church that charges for grace has forgotten Easter; a Church that gives freely is preaching the Resurrection without saying a word.
conn: The barren one sings.

“Sing, O barren one who did not bear” (Isaiah 54:1); Hannah sings when the barren woman bears (1 Samuel 2:5); Paul applies Isaiah's song to the Jerusalem above, “and she is our mother” (Galatians 4:26–27).
The oath of Noah.

God set his bow in the clouds as a sign of the covenant (Genesis 9:13); he swears by the days of Noah that his steadfast love will not depart (Isaiah 54:9–10); Peter sees in the flood a figure of Baptism (1 Peter 3:20–21).
Seven helpers full of the Spirit.

Moses was given seventy elders to share the burden, with the spirit that was on him (Numbers 11:16–17); the apostles are given seven men full of the Spirit and of wisdom (Acts 6:3); Paul names the qualities of deacons (1 Timothy 3:8–13).
Care for the widow.
God is “Father of orphans and protector of widows” (Psalm 68:5); pure religion is “to care for orphans and widows in their distress” (James 1:27).
Buried and raised.
“we have been buried with him by baptism into death” (Romans 6:4); “you were also raised with him through faith” (Colossians 2:12).
Sent with authority.
Jesus calls the Twelve and sends them out two by two (Mark 6:7); after the Resurrection he sends them to all nations (Matthew 28:19–20).
altar: At every Holy Qurbana the deacon stands between the altar and the people, calling us to prayer, to attention and to peace. His service at the altar is the same service the seven gave at the tables of the widows: the Lord who feeds us asks us to feed others.
Nothing on the altar is bought. The bread and wine we offer become, by the Holy Spirit, the true Body and Blood of Christ, given to us without payment. We receive freely so that we may give freely.
outline: Opening
A widow in a back pew whom nobody has visited since the funeral.
Point 1 · Enlarge your tent
The barren one sings: Easter makes the Church a mother of many.
Point 2 · Seven men full of the Spirit
Serving tables and serving the word.
Point 3 · Nailed to the cross
The record against us erased; the powers disarmed.
Point 4 · Give without payment
The Twelve sent with empty bags and full hands.
Closing image
The seven kneeling while the apostles lay hands on them.
Take-home line
“You received without payment; give without payment.”
live: Visit a widow or widower (Acts 6:1)
This week visit, telephone or bring food to one widow or widower in your family or parish who may feel forgotten.
Give freely (Matthew 10:8)
Do one service this week for which you will receive no payment and no thanks.
Pray for deacons
Pray today for the deacons and the seminarians of your eparchy, and for one young man you know who may be called.
Remember your Baptism (Colossians 2:12)
Find the date of your Baptism, and on that day each year light a candle and thank God.
fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Christ sent the apostles without gold or bag so that their very poverty would preach. Freed from all anxiety about food and clothing, they could give themselves wholly to the word, and the people who saw them could not suspect them of seeking gain. He gave them the power to raise the dead and told them to give it freely, so that their gift would match the gift they had received.
St Augustine (in substance)

The barren woman who is told to sing is the Church gathered from the nations. She who seemed to have no children now gives birth every year in the font, and she has more children than the synagogue of old, not by human strength but by the grace of God who makes the barren a joyful mother.
magis: Catechism 1569–1571
Deacons are ordained not to the priesthood but to the ministry; they serve at the altar, in the proclamation of the Gospel and in works of charity.
Catechism 858–859
Jesus called the Twelve and sent them; the apostles are the envoys of Christ, and their mission continues in the Church.
Catechism 628
Baptism signifies the descent into the tomb of the Christian, who dies to sin with Christ in order to live a new life.
Catechism 2443–2444
God blesses those who come to the aid of the poor; the Church's love for the poor is part of her constant tradition.
Catechism 1972
The New Law is called a law of love, a law of grace and a law of freedom.
saints: Easter week

Thursday 1 April is the First Thursday of Resurrection. Tomorrow, Friday 2 April, the Syro-Malabar calendar keeps the Feast of Martyrs, in the East Syriac tradition the commemoration of all the saints (verify locally). Sunday 4 April: New Sunday (Puthu Njayar).
2027-04-01.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you widen the tent of your Church and give her children she never expected. Thank you for the grace we received without payment: our Baptism, your forgiveness, your Body and Blood. Make us generous with what we have received. Bless the deacons of your Church and all who serve at the tables of the poor; let no widow be neglected among us. Send us, as you sent the Twelve, to bring your peace into every house we enter. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-04-02.title: First Friday of Resurrection: the Feast of Martyrs
2027-04-02.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The prayer of Azariah in the furnace
The ancestors who bore witness by faith
2027-04-02.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The Feast of Martyrs: in the East Syriac tradition the Friday after Easter is the feast of all the saints, the martyrs and confessors (verify locally). It is also the First Friday of the month. There is no abstinence on this first Friday after Easter. The calendar notes the fuller passages: Daniel 3:25–45, Acts 6:8–7:10, Hebrews 11:3–10, 32–12:2 and Matthew 10:16–33. The prayer in the furnace belongs to the Greek part of Daniel 3, and Bibles number these verses differently.
2027-04-02.verse: Everyone therefore who acknowledges me before others, I also will acknowledge before my Father in heaven.
theo: On the first Friday after Easter the Church of the East keeps the feast of all the saints, and above all of the martyrs. The placing is deliberate. The martyrs are those who went with Christ through death into life, and so their feast belongs in the week of the Resurrection, not in the gloom of a funeral. The East Syriac tradition explains the day by its own history. In the fourth century the Persian king Shapur II launched a long persecution against the Christians of his empire. Mar Shemun bar Sabbae, Catholicos of Seleucia-Ctesiphon, refused to betray his flock or to worship the sun, and by tradition he was put to death on Good Friday, about the year 341 or 344, together with a great company of bishops, priests and faithful. Since Good Friday could not become a feast, the martyrs came to be remembered on the Friday after Easter: so the tradition tells it. The Church of St Thomas in India received this calendar and this memory, and the Syro-Malabar Church still keeps the day as the Feast of Martyrs. The witnesses have not stopped. Blessed Rani Maria Vattalil, a Franciscan Clarist sister from Pulluvazhy in Kerala, was stabbed to death on a bus near Indore in 1995, killed in hatred of the faith, stirred up by her work among the poor, and was beatified in 2017. Her family later forgave the man who killed her, and he came to their home to ask their pardon. A martyr's blood, and a martyr's family's forgiveness, preach the Resurrection more loudly than any sermon.

The first reading takes us into a furnace. Three young Jews in Babylon, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, have refused to worship the golden statue. Before they are thrown into the fire they give the king an answer that every martyr has repeated: “If our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the furnace of blazing fire and out of your hand, O king, let him deliver us. But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods and we will not worship the golden statue that you have set up.” (Daniel 3:17–18). Then the astonishing scene: “They walked around in the midst of the flames, singing hymns to God and blessing the Lord.” Azariah stands still in the fire and prays, and his prayer is not a complaint but a confession: “Blessed are you, O Lord, God of our ancestors, and worthy of praise; and glorious is your name forever! For you are just in all you have done.” He does not accuse God of injustice; he accepts that his people have sinned and still trusts in God's mercy. The king, looking in, sees four men walking unbound in the fire, and the fourth looks like a son of the gods. Many Fathers saw in that fourth figure the Son of God, who does not take his witnesses out of the fire but walks with them in it. This is how the martyrs have died: singing, forgiving, and not alone.

In Acts we meet the first Christian martyr. “Stephen, full of grace and power, did great wonders and signs among the people.” Some members of one synagogue in Jerusalem argue with him, “But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke.” False witnesses are found to accuse him of speaking against the Temple and the law. Stephen was himself a Jew, as were the apostles and the whole first community; the quarrel was within one family, and the Church, following the Second Vatican Council (Nostra Aetate 4), never reads such passages as a charge against the Jewish people. What Luke wants us to see is the face of the witness: “And all who sat in the council looked intently at him, and they saw that his face was like the face of an angel.” Like Moses coming down from Sinai, Stephen's face shines because he has been with God. Soon he will see heaven opened, pray for his killers and die (Acts 7:56–60). The Letter to the Hebrews then opens the great roll of the witnesses of faith. “By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain's... he died, but through his faith he still speaks.” By faith Noah built the ark. “By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to set out for a place that he was to receive as an inheritance; and he set out, not knowing where he was going.” These men and women did not see the promise fulfilled, “For he looked forward to the city that has foundations, whose architect and builder is God.” The martyrs are the ones who believed the city was real enough to die for.

The Gospel is Jesus' instruction to witnesses. Three times he says, Do not be afraid. “So have no fear of them; for nothing is covered up that will not be uncovered.” “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul.” “So do not be afraid; you are of more value than many sparrows.” The reason is the tenderness of the Father: “Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. And even the hairs of your head are all counted.” Then the promise and the warning: “Everyone therefore who acknowledges me before others, I also will acknowledge before my Father in heaven; but whoever denies me before others, I also will deny before my Father in heaven.” The Syriac word for martyr, sahda, like the Greek martys, means simply a witness. Few of us will be asked to die for Christ, but all of us are asked to acknowledge him: at the office table, in the hostel, in the family group chat, in the way we do business and the way we speak of the poor. Today is also the First Friday, the day many families give to the Sacred Heart. The Heart that was pierced on the Cross and rose glorified is the source of every martyr's courage. To keep this feast well is to ask for a little of that courage, and to make one small act of acknowledgement before the day ends.
conn: The fourth man in the fire.
“When you walk through fire you shall not be burned” (Isaiah 43:2); the king sees four men walking unbound in the furnace (Daniel 3:92, in Catholic numbering); “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).
Faces that shine.

Moses' face shone because he had been talking with God (Exodus 34:29); Stephen's face was “like the face of an angel” (Acts 6:15); at the Transfiguration Jesus' face “shone like the sun” (Matthew 17:2).
The first martyr prays as his Master.
Jesus prays, “Father, forgive them” and “into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:34, 46); Stephen prays, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” and “do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:59–60).
The cloud of witnesses.
The roll of faith in Hebrews 11 ends with “so great a cloud of witnesses” (Hebrews 12:1); John sees a great multitude “robed in white, with palm branches in their hands” (Revelation 7:9).
Precious death.
“Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his faithful ones” (Psalm 116:15); “the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God” (Wisdom 3:1).
Blessed when persecuted.
“Blessed are you when people revile you and persecute you” (Matthew 5:11); “they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony” (Revelation 12:11).
altar: From the earliest centuries the Holy Qurbana was offered over the tombs of the martyrs, and relics of saints are still placed in our altars. The martyrs gave their bodies for Christ because Christ first gave his Body for them; at the altar their sacrifice is joined to his.
Each time we receive Communion we say Amen to the Body of Christ in front of everyone. It is the smallest act of witness, and the martyrs began with the same Amen.
outline: Opening
A bus near Indore, 1995, and a family that forgave.
Point 1 · But if not
Three young men walk singing in the fire.
Point 2 · The face of an angel
Stephen, full of grace and power.
Point 3 · By faith
Abel, Noah and Abraham, the witnesses who still speak.
Point 4 · Do not be afraid
Sparrows, counted hairs and acknowledging Christ.
Closing image
A great multitude robed in white, with palm branches.
Take-home line
“Everyone therefore who acknowledges me before others, I also will acknowledge before my Father in heaven.”
live: Acknowledge Christ (Matthew 10:32)
Make one quiet act of acknowledgement today: say grace in a public place, or speak of your faith when the subject comes up.
Pray for persecuted Christians
Pray today, by name if you can, for a country where Christians are suffering for their faith.
Keep the First Friday
Go to the Sacrament of Reconciliation or make an act of reparation to the Sacred Heart today.
Forgive like the martyrs (Acts 7:60)
Pray Stephen's prayer for one person who has hurt you: Lord, do not hold this against them.
fathers: Aphrahat the Persian Sage, Demonstration on Persecution (in substance)

Writing during the persecution of Shapur, Aphrahat recalled that the righteous have always been persecuted: Abel by his brother, Jacob by Esau, Joseph by his brothers, Moses by Pharaoh, David by Saul, Daniel by the satraps, the three young men by Nebuchadnezzar. Last of all Jesus was persecuted and crucified. So the Church should not be surprised by suffering; she walks the road of the righteous, and her Lord walks it before her.
St Augustine (in substance)

It is not the punishment but the cause that makes the martyr. Many suffer, but the martyr suffers for Christ and for the truth. Let us honour the martyrs by imitating their cause, not by seeking their pain, and by loving the One for whom they died.
magis: Catechism 2473–2474
Martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith; the Church has carefully gathered the records of those who persevered to the end.
Catechism 957
Communion with the saints joins us to Christ; we venerate the martyrs and saints as disciples and imitators of the Lord.
Catechism 1173
In the yearly cycle the Church commemorates the martyrs and saints, proclaiming the Paschal mystery in those who suffered and were glorified with Christ.
Catechism 145–147
Hebrews 11 celebrates the faith of the ancestors; Abraham is the model of obedient faith.
Catechism 2471
Before Pilate Christ bore witness to the truth; the Christian must not be ashamed of testifying to the Lord.
saints: Today

2 April: the Feast of Martyrs. The East Syriac Churches remember on this Friday all the martyrs and confessors, among them Mar Shemun bar Sabbae, Catholicos of Seleucia-Ctesiphon, and his companions, put to death under the Persian king Shapur II in the fourth century (by tradition on Good Friday, about 341 or 344; verify locally how your eparchy keeps the day).
2027-04-02.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, first-born from the dead and faithful witness, you walked with the three young men in the fire and showed your glory to Stephen as he died. We thank you for all the martyrs and saints of your Church, for Mar Shemun and his companions, for the witnesses of our own land and our own time. Give us their courage to acknowledge you before others, their faith to go out not knowing where we are going, and their love to forgive those who hurt us. With Mary, Queen of Martyrs, who stood beside your Cross, let us one day join the great multitude robed in white. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-04-03.title: First Saturday of Resurrection
2027-04-03.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-04-03.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The last day of the first week of the Resurrection, the week of the newly baptised. Tomorrow is New Sunday (Puthu Njayar), the Second Sunday of Resurrection.
2027-04-03.verse: For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
theo: On the last day of Easter week the Church goes back once more to the tomb, this time with Mark. “When the sabbath was over, Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices, so that they might go and anoint him.” They are going to do the last thing love can do for the dead. On the way they have one worry: “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance to the tomb?” It is a real problem; Mark tells us the stone “was very large”. But “When they looked up, they saw that the stone, which was very large, had already been rolled back.” How much of our life is spent walking towards a stone that God has already moved. We lie awake over a conversation we fear, a sin we cannot confess, a reconciliation we think impossible, and when we finally arrive, the stone is gone. Inside the tomb a young man in a white robe gives the Easter announcement: “Do not be alarmed; you are looking for Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has been raised; he is not here. Look, there is the place they laid him.” The angel points to an empty place. The Church has never preached a Resurrection of the spirit only, or a Christ who lives on merely in the memory of his friends. The body that was laid there is gone because it has been raised, the same body that bore the nails, now glorified. The Gospels do not tell us that the Risen Lord appeared first to his Mother, but an old and loving tradition of the Church, among Eastern and Western writers alike, has believed that he did, and that Mary, who kept faith through the long Saturday, was the first to be filled with the joy of her Son's Resurrection.

Then the commission: “But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going ahead of you to Galilee; there you will see him, just as he told you.” Two words have consoled sinners for twenty centuries: and Peter. Peter, who had sworn he did not know the man; Peter, who had wept in the courtyard. He is named on purpose, so that he will not think he has been struck off the list. The Risen Lord does not send a message to the faithful disciples and leave out the one who failed. And he sends them back to Galilee, where it all began, by the lake where he first called them. He is “going ahead of you”: wherever we go, he is there first. Mark's Gospel then ends in a strange way: “So they went out and fled from the tomb, for terror and amazement had seized them; and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.” The oldest manuscripts of Mark stop here; the Church receives the longer ending (Mark 16:9–20) as inspired Scripture, and it tells of the appearances that followed. But the silence of verse 8 is itself a message. The news was too great for them at first; fear held them. Yet we know the end of the story: the women did speak, the disciples did see him in Galilee, and the news has reached Kerala and every continent. Fear was not the last word. Every Christian who hears the Easter Gospel is asked to finish the sentence the women left unfinished, by telling someone.

Paul tells the newly baptised what to do with the Easter news in daily life. “So if you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth.” This is not an escape from the world; Paul goes on in the same chapter to speak of family life, work and forgiveness. It is a question of where the heart is fixed. Every Holy Qurbana, before the great prayer of the anaphora, the priest calls us to lift up our minds on high, and we answer that they are turned towards the God of Abraham, Isaac and Israel. Then the deepest line: “for you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ who is your life is revealed, then you also will be revealed with him in glory.” Tomorrow, on New Sunday, the newly baptised of the ancient Church laid aside the white garments they had worn all week. The white robe was put away, but the new life was not; it went on, hidden, like a seed under the soil, like a treasure in a locked box, like the life of the Lord himself for thirty years at Nazareth. Most of the holiness in the world is hidden: a mother's prayers for a son abroad, a nurse's patience on a night shift, an old man's rosary in an empty church. None of it is lost. It is hidden with Christ in God, and on the last day it will be revealed with him in glory.
conn: The stone rolled away.
An angel rolls back the stone and sits on it (Matthew 28:2); the stone was “very large” (Mark 16:4); “Weeping may linger for the night, but joy comes with the morning” (Psalm 30:5).
The first day of the week.

God began creation on the first day (Genesis 1:3–5); the women come “very early on the first day of the week” (Mark 16:2); the first Christians gathered on the first day of the week to break bread (Acts 20:7).
And Peter.
Jesus prayed that Peter's faith would not fail (Luke 22:31–32); Peter wept after his denial (Luke 22:61–62); the Risen Lord asks him three times, “do you love me?” (John 21:15–17).
Back to Galilee.

“Galilee of the Gentiles… the people who sat in darkness have seen a great light” (Matthew 4:15–16); the Risen Lord meets the Eleven on a mountain in Galilee and sends them to all nations (Matthew 28:16–20).
Seated at the right hand.
“The LORD says to my lord, ‘Sit at my right hand’” (Psalm 110:1); Stephen sees Jesus standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7:56).
The hidden life.
“he will hide me in his shelter in the day of trouble” (Psalm 27:5); “your Father who sees in secret will reward you” (Matthew 6:6).
