altar: The women came with spices for a dead body and found the Living One. At the Holy Qurbana we do not come to honour a memory: the Lord who rose bodily from the tomb gives us his true Body and Blood, alive and glorified.

Before the anaphora the priest invites us to lift up our minds on high. To seek the things that are above, Paul's Easter command, is what we do at every Qurbana, where heaven and earth meet on the altar.
outline: Opening
A woman lying awake over a conversation she dreads.
Point 1 · Who will roll away the stone?
The women's worry and the stone already moved.
Point 2 · He has been raised; he is not here
The empty place and the bodily Resurrection.
Point 3 · Tell his disciples and Peter
The one who failed is named first.
Point 4 · Hidden with Christ in God
Seeking the things above; the hidden holiness of every day.
Closing image
White baptismal robes folded and put away, and a life that goes on.
Take-home line
“Your life is hidden with Christ in God.”
live: Walk towards the stone (Mark 16:3)
Take one step this week towards a reconciliation or a confession you have been dreading; trust that God goes before you.
Remember Peter (Mark 16:7)
If you feel you have failed God, read Mark 16:7 slowly and put your own name after ‘and’.
Lift up your mind (Colossians 3:2)
Before you open your phone in the morning, lift your mind to God with one short prayer.
Honour hidden holiness
Thank one person this week whose quiet faithfulness nobody notices.
fathers: St Gregory the Great (in substance)

Why did the angel name Peter alone? Because if he had not been named, Peter, who had denied his Master, might have thought himself unworthy to come among the disciples. So he is called by name, so that he may not despair because of his denial. Let us consider how great is the mercy of God, who does not let the fallen be lost but calls him back by name.
St Augustine (in substance)

When you hear, Lift up your hearts, and you answer that you have them lifted up to the Lord, let your answer be true. Our Head has gone up into heaven; let the members follow in desire. While the body is still on earth, the heart can already be where Christ is, and our life is hidden there with him until he appears.
magis: Catechism 640
The empty tomb and the linen cloths lying there signify that the body of Christ escaped the bonds of death by God's power.
Catechism 641
Mary Magdalene and the holy women were the first to encounter the Risen One and the first messengers of the Resurrection, even to the apostles.
Catechism 642
Peter, chosen to confirm the faith of his brothers, saw the Risen One before them; on his witness the community exclaims, ‘The Lord has risen indeed’.
Catechism 655
The Resurrection of Christ is the principle and source of our future resurrection.
Catechism 1002–1003
United with Christ by Baptism, believers already share in his risen life; but this life remains hidden with Christ in God.
saints: Easter week

Saturday 3 April closes the first week of Resurrection, the week of the newly baptised. Tomorrow, Sunday 4 April: New Sunday (Puthu Njayar), the confession of St Thomas, and in many places the great pilgrimage to the Kurisumudi at Malayattoor.
2027-04-03.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you rolled away the stone that we feared, and you left the tomb empty because you are risen in the body. You sent word to your disciples and to Peter, so that no one who has failed would think himself forgotten. Raise our minds to the things that are above, where you are seated at the right hand of the Father. Keep our life hidden with you in God, and when you appear, let us appear with you in glory. Through the prayers of your holy Mother, who kept faith through the long Saturday, fill us with Easter joy. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-04-05.title: Second Monday of Resurrection
2027-04-05.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The disciples recognise the Risen Christ
2027-04-05.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The second week of the Resurrection begins. The Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost. The Latin Church keeps the Annunciation of the Lord today, moved from 25 March, which fell on Pesaha Thursday; the Syro-Malabar First Set gives no transfer, so follow the direction of your eparchy.
2027-04-05.verse: Then their eyes were opened, and they recognized him; and he vanished from their sight.
theo: The Easter octave is over, and the Church goes back to ordinary Mondays: to work, to school, to the market and the bus stand. The readings of this second week of the Resurrection are chosen for exactly that return. They ask what Easter looks like in a parish with quarrels, in a family with tensions, on a road walked by two tired disciples. Paul begins with a parish that had split into fan clubs. News has reached him through Chloe's household: “there are quarrels among you, my brothers and sisters. What I mean is that each of you says, ‘I belong to Paul,’ or ‘I belong to Apollos,’ or ‘I belong to Cephas,’ or ‘I belong to Christ.’” Each group had chosen its favourite preacher, and even the people who said ‘I belong to Christ’ had turned the Lord into a party badge. Paul answers with three short questions that cut through everything: “Has Christ been divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” There is only one Lord who died for us and only one name into which we were baptised. Paul even thanks God that he baptised very few of them, so that no one could claim to belong to him. His task was something else: “For Christ did not send me to baptize but to proclaim the gospel, and not with eloquent wisdom, so that the cross of Christ might not be emptied of its power.” A Church that argues about its preachers has forgotten its Crucified and Risen Lord. Unity is not a matter of everyone liking the same priest or the same style; it is the fruit of looking together at the Cross and the empty tomb.

The Gospel takes us back to the evening of Easter Sunday, on the road to Emmaus. Two disciples have walked seven miles with a stranger who explained the Scriptures to them. Now they reach their village, and “he walked ahead as if he were going on.” The Risen Lord never forces his company on anyone. He waits to be invited. “But they urged him strongly, saying, ‘Stay with us, because it is almost evening and the day is now nearly over.’ So he went in to stay with them.” That prayer, Stay with us, has been on Christian lips ever since; it is the prayer of every evening and of every life that feels the light going. Then comes the moment the whole story was moving towards: “When he was at the table with them, he took bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to them. Then their eyes were opened, and they recognized him; and he vanished from their sight.” The four verbs are the verbs of the Last Supper, and of every Holy Qurbana: he took, blessed, broke and gave. They knew him not by his face but by what he did with bread. And as soon as they knew him, he was no longer visible in the old way, because from now on he would be present to them in the breaking of the bread.

What happens next is the shape of the Christian life. “They said to each other, ‘Were not our hearts burning within us while he was talking to us on the road, while he was opening the scriptures to us?’ That same hour they got up and returned to Jerusalem.” It was night, and it was seven miles, but the burning heart cannot wait till morning. They find the community gathered, and before they can tell their news they are told: “The Lord has risen indeed, and he has appeared to Simon!” Then they share their own story: “how he had been made known to them in the breaking of the bread.” Notice the movement: away from Jerusalem in sadness, back to Jerusalem in joy; from two scattered disciples to the gathered Church around Peter. The Risen Lord heals divisions not by argument but by gathering his people at one table. Paul's quarrelling Corinthians and the two lonely disciples need the same cure. In the Syro-Malabar Holy Qurbana, after the anaphora, the priest breaks the Holy Bread and signs the Precious Blood with it, uniting them again: the Body broken and the Blood poured out are joined, because the One who died is alive. Every parish that gathers at that altar is being made one, quarrels and all.
conn: One Lord, one baptism.
“There is one body and one Spirit… one Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Ephesians 4:4–5); Jesus prays “that they may all be one” (John 17:21).
The cross not emptied.
Paul will say a few verses later, “we proclaim Christ crucified” (1 Corinthians 1:23); in Galatians, “May I never boast of anything except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6:14).
Stay with us.
Abraham urges the three visitors at Mamre, “do not pass by your servant” (Genesis 18:3), and entertains the Lord unawares; “some have entertained angels without knowing it” (Hebrews 13:2).
Took, blessed, broke, gave.
The same four actions at the feeding of the five thousand (Luke 9:16) and at the Last Supper (Luke 22:19).
Hearts burning.
Jeremiah felt the word of God “like a burning fire shut up in my bones” (Jeremiah 20:9).
Appeared to Simon.
Paul hands on the same early witness: “he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve” (1 Corinthians 15:5).
altar: At every Holy Qurbana the road to Emmaus is walked again: first the Lord opens the Scriptures to us, then he takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it and gives it. He is truly present, Body and Blood, soul and divinity, under the signs of bread and wine.
The breaking of the Holy Bread after the anaphora, and its signing with the Precious Blood, proclaim the one Christ, crucified and risen. Around that one Bread a divided people is made one body.
outline: Opening
Back to an ordinary Monday after the Easter octave.
Point 1 · Has Christ been divided?
Paul and the parish of fan clubs.
Point 2 · Stay with us
The Lord who waits to be invited.
Point 3 · Known in the breaking of the bread
Took, blessed, broke, gave.
Point 4 · That same hour
The burning heart runs back to the community.
Closing image
Two travellers turning round in the dark and walking seven miles back with joy.
Take-home line
“Stay with us, because it is almost evening.”
live: Mend one division (1 Corinthians 1:10)
Speak kindly this week to someone in your parish or family from whom you have drifted apart.
Pray the Emmaus prayer (Luke 24:29)
Each evening before sleep, say: Lord, stay with us, because it is almost evening.
Come to the breaking of the bread
Attend one weekday Holy Qurbana this week, and listen to the readings as the two disciples listened on the road.
Share your Easter story
Tell one person how the Lord has made himself known to you.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

Where did the Lord wish to be recognised? In the breaking of bread. We are secure: we break bread, and we recognise the Lord. He did not want to be known except there, for our sake, who would not see him in the flesh but would eat his flesh. So whoever you are who believe, do not despair because you did not see him then: you have him in the breaking of the bread.
St Gregory the Great (in substance)

They did not know him while he explained the Scriptures, but they knew him when they gave him bread. The truth is learned not only by hearing the commandments of God but by doing them. They welcomed a stranger to their table, and found that the stranger was God.
magis: Catechism 1329
The Eucharist is called the Breaking of Bread, because Jesus used this rite as master of the table, and by this action his disciples recognised him after his Resurrection.
Catechism 1347
The Emmaus meal is the pattern of the liturgy: the Lord explains the Scriptures, then takes bread, blesses and breaks it.
Catechism 820
Christ bestowed unity on his Church from the beginning; the Church must always pray and work to keep, strengthen and perfect it.
Catechism 817
Divisions wound the unity of Christ's Body; they arise from human sin and must be healed by conversion and charity.
saints: This week

Monday 5 to Saturday 10 April: the second week of the Resurrection. Sunday 11 April: the Third Sunday of Resurrection. The Latin Church keeps the Annunciation of the Lord on Monday 5 April this year (moved from 25 March, which fell on Pesaha Thursday); Syro-Malabar faithful follow the direction of their eparchy.
2027-04-05.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you walked with your disciples on the road and made yourself known to them in the breaking of the bread. Stay with us, for it is almost evening. Open the Scriptures to us, set our hearts on fire, and heal the divisions in our parishes and families, so that we may be one in you, who were crucified for us and live for ever with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-04-06.title: Second Tuesday of Resurrection
2027-04-06.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-04-06.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost.
2027-04-06.verse: If you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me.
theo: A few days earlier Saul of Tarsus had been on the road to Damascus with letters from the high priest, ready to arrest anyone who belonged to the Way. Then a light flashed from heaven, a voice asked, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?’, and he was led blind into the city. After three days Ananias laid hands on him, the scales fell from his eyes, and he was baptised. Today's reading begins at that point, and its first word is the most surprising: “immediately he began to proclaim Jesus in the synagogues, saying, ‘He is the Son of God.’” There was no long apprenticeship, no waiting to become respectable. The man who came to Damascus to silence the name of Jesus now cannot stop speaking it. The people who hear him are astonished: “Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem among those who invoked this name?” The Resurrection does not only raise a dead body in Jerusalem; it raises dead hearts on the road to Damascus. Luke adds: “Saul became increasingly more powerful and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Messiah.” Saul is himself a Jew, preaching in the synagogue, reasoning from the Scriptures of Israel. This is an argument within the one family of Abraham about the Messiah of Israel, and the Church reads it with that love, never as a charge against the Jewish people.

Then comes danger. “After some time had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him, but their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night so that they might kill him; but his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket.” Paul himself tells the same story years later in Second Corinthians, adding that the governor under King Aretas also guarded the city. And he tells it in the middle of a list of his weaknesses, as the thing he chooses to boast of. The great apostle, who would one day stand before kings, begins his ministry squeezed into a basket and lowered down a wall at night by his new brothers. He did not save himself; he was carried by the community he had come to destroy. There is an Easter lesson here for every proud heart: the Risen Lord makes us strong, but often he does it by first making us small, and by teaching us to depend on our brothers and sisters in faith.

In the Gospel Jesus is in Jerusalem, in a long debate after healing a man on the sabbath. He speaks to some who oppose him, and his words go deep: “I do not accept glory from human beings.” Then he puts his finger on what makes faith impossible: “How can you believe when you accept glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the one who alone is God?” Faith dies where people live for the applause of others. Then Jesus names Moses, the great lawgiver whom his hearers loved: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me.” Moses is not set aside; he is called as a witness. The Law, the Psalms and the Prophets all speak of Christ. That is why the Church never throws away the Old Testament: it is the word of God, and in it Christ is hidden, waiting to be found. On the evening of Easter the Risen Lord himself, “beginning with Moses and all the prophets” (Luke 24:27), opened the Scriptures to the disciples on the road. In the Syro-Malabar Holy Qurbana on Sundays and feasts, a reading from the Law or the Prophets comes before the Apostle and the Gospel: Moses and the prophets still speak in our churches, and they still speak of him. The question Jesus asks is for us too: do we seek the glory that comes from God, or the glory that comes from one another?
conn: Paul's own account.
“I went away at once into Arabia, and afterwards I returned to Damascus” (Galatians 1:17); “I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall” (2 Corinthians 11:33).
You are my son.
“He said to me, ‘You are my son; today I have begotten you’” (Psalm 2:7); Paul preaches this psalm as fulfilled in the Resurrection (Acts 13:33).
A prophet like Moses.
“The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your own people” (Deuteronomy 18:15); Peter applies it to Jesus (Acts 3:22).
About whom Moses wrote.
Philip tells Nathanael, “We have found him about whom Moses in the law and also the prophets wrote” (John 1:45).
Beginning with Moses.
On the road to Emmaus the Risen Lord interprets “the things about himself in all the scriptures” (Luke 24:27).
The glory from God.
“For the LORD does not see as mortals see; they look on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Law, the Prophets, the Apostle and the Gospel are read before the anaphora: the whole of Scripture leads us to the altar, where the One of whom Moses wrote gives himself as the true Bread from heaven.
Saul was carried in a basket by his brothers; at the altar we too are carried, by the prayer of the whole Church, to the Lord who makes the weak strong.
outline: Opening
The persecutor who cannot stop speaking the name.
Point 1 · He is the Son of God
Immediately, in the synagogues.
Point 2 · Lowered in a basket
Strength that begins with being carried.
Point 3 · The glory that comes from God
Why applause kills faith.
Point 4 · Moses wrote about me
Christ hidden in the Old Testament.
Closing image
A basket swinging down a city wall at night, and a church that carries its weak.
Take-home line
“He wrote about me.”
live: Speak the name (Acts 9:20)
Say a good word about Jesus this week to someone who does not expect it from you.
Let yourself be carried
Ask someone in your parish to pray for a difficulty you have been carrying alone.
Seek God's glory (John 5:44)
Do one good thing this week secretly, telling no one.
Read Moses with Christ
Read Deuteronomy 18:15–19 and John 1:45 together, and ask where Christ is in the Law.
fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)

See how Paul did not wait. He did not say, ‘Let me first learn and then teach,’ but at once he went into the synagogues, the very places where he had been ready to bind Christians, and there he preached Christ. The wolf had become a shepherd, and the one who came to scatter now gathered.
St Jerome (in substance)
Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ. Whoever reads Moses and the prophets with faith finds Christ in every page, as the disciples did when he opened their minds.
magis: Catechism 442

From the beginning, the confession of Jesus as the Son of God stands at the centre of the apostolic faith; Paul, after his conversion, at once proclaimed in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God.
Catechism 129
Christians read the Old Testament in the light of Christ crucified and risen; the New Testament lies hidden in the Old and the Old is made manifest in the New.
Catechism 121
The Old Testament is an indispensable part of Sacred Scripture; its books are divinely inspired and retain a permanent value, for the Old Covenant has never been revoked.
Catechism 839
The Jewish faith, unlike other non-Christian religions, is already a response to God's revelation in the Old Covenant; to the Jewish people belong the sonship, the covenants and the promises.

2027-04-06.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, you turned Saul the persecutor into Paul the apostle, and you were proclaimed by him in the synagogues of Damascus. Open our eyes as you opened his, and our lips to speak your name. Deliver us from seeking the glory that comes from one another, and teach us to seek only the glory that comes from God. Open to us the Law and the Prophets, so that in every page we may find you, risen and living for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-04-07.title: Second Wednesday of Resurrection
2027-04-07.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-04-07.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost.
2027-04-07.verse: They were astounded beyond measure, saying, “He has done everything well; he even makes the deaf to hear and the mute to speak.”
theo: Paul's letter to the Galatians is the most passionate thing he ever wrote, and today's reading opens with its battle-cry: “For freedom Christ has set us free. Stand firm, therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery.” The Galatians were Gentiles who had come to faith in the Risen Christ through Paul's preaching. Then teachers arrived who told them that faith and Baptism were not enough: to belong fully to God's people, the men must also be circumcised and the whole Law of Moses taken up. Paul's answer is fierce because so much is at stake. If a Gentile must first become a Jew in order to be saved by Christ, then Christ's death and Resurrection are not enough, and grace has become a reward to be earned. “You who want to be justified by the law have cut yourselves off from Christ; you have fallen away from grace.” Paul is not attacking the Jewish people or their faithful observance of the covenant God gave them; he himself was a Jew who loved the Law. He is defending the truth that the Gentiles are welcomed into the family of Abraham by grace, through faith in the Risen Lord. Easter is liberation: the Lord who broke the chains of death does not hand us a new set of chains.

But freedom in Christ is not freedom to do as we please. Paul ends with a sentence that holds together what Christians have too often pulled apart: “For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything; the only thing that counts is faith working through love.” Faith is not a private opinion that leaves life unchanged; it works, and the work it does is love. The Catholic faith has always insisted on both halves: we are saved by grace through faith, not by our own merits; and the faith that saves is living faith, which shows itself in love. As Saint James says, “faith by itself, if it has no works, is dead” (James 2:17). A few verses later in Galatians Paul will say that the whole law is summed up in a single commandment, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Christian freedom is the freedom of a son or daughter in the Father's house, no longer working for wages but serving out of love.

The Gospel takes Jesus into the Decapolis, the ten Greek-speaking cities on the far side of the Sea of Galilee, a largely Gentile region. There “they brought to him a deaf man who had an impediment in his speech.” Mark describes every gesture with care. Jesus “took him aside in private, away from the crowd,” as if to spare him embarrassment; he puts his fingers into his ears, spits and touches his tongue; then, “looking up to heaven, he sighed and said to him, ‘Ephphatha,’ that is, ‘Be opened.’” The Lord who could heal with a word chooses to heal with touch, with his own body. These are already sacramental signs: God's grace comes to us through what can be seen and touched. “And immediately his ears were opened, his tongue was released, and he spoke plainly.” In the ancient Church this Gospel was acted out at Baptism: the bishop touched the ears and mouth of the one to be baptised and said, Ephphatha, so that the newly baptised might hear the word of God and speak his praise. The Latin rite of Baptism still keeps it. The crowd's cry, “He has done everything well,” echoes the first page of the Bible, where God saw everything he had made and it was very good. In the Risen Christ creation is being made new. In the Syro-Malabar Holy Qurbana, before the Gospel is proclaimed, the people sing Halleluia: ears opened to hear the Gospel, tongues loosed to praise.
conn: Out of the house of slavery.
“I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exodus 20:2); “if the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8:36).
Faith that works.
“So faith by itself, if it has no works, is dead” (James 2:17); “the whole law is summed up in a single commandment, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’” (Galatians 5:14).
All one in Christ.
“There is no longer Jew or Greek… for all of you are one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28).
The ears of the deaf unstopped.
Isaiah foretold, “the ears of the deaf unstopped… and the tongue of the speechless sing for joy” (Isaiah 35:5–6); Jesus points to these signs for John the Baptist (Luke 7:22).
Open my lips.
“O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will declare your praise” (Psalm 51:15).
Very good.
“God saw everything that he had made, and indeed, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31); the crowd says, “He has done everything well” (Mark 7:37).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Lord still heals through signs: bread and wine become his true Body and Blood, and he touches us with them, opening our ears to his word and our lips to his praise.
The faith we profess in the Creed becomes faith working through love when we carry the Qurbana out of the church into our homes and streets.
outline: Opening
Freedom is the first word of Easter.
Point 1 · For freedom Christ has set us free
Do not take up the yoke again.
Point 2 · Faith working through love
Grace that bears fruit.
Point 3 · Ephphatha
The Lord heals with touch and word.
Point 4 · He has done everything well
Creation made new in the Risen Christ.
Closing image
A catechist signing the Our Father to a deaf child before First Holy Communion.
Take-home line
“Ephphatha: Be opened.”
live: Stand firm in freedom (Galatians 5:1)
Name one habit that enslaves you, and bring it to confession during this Easter season.
Let faith work (Galatians 5:6)
Do one concrete act of love this week for someone who cannot repay you.
Be opened (Mark 7:34)
Before the Gospel at Holy Qurbana, pray silently: Lord, open my ears and my lips.
Remember the deaf
Find out whether your parish or diocese has a ministry for deaf people, and support it.
fathers: St Ambrose (in substance)

To the newly baptised: open your ears and receive the mysteries. When the bishop touched your ears and nostrils, he did what Christ did in the Gospel for the deaf man, saying, Ephphatha, be opened. He did this so that your ears might be opened to the word and the speech of the Lord.
St Augustine (in substance)

The demons also believe, and tremble; but their faith does not save them, because it does not love. The faith that the apostle praises is faith working through love: this is the faith of Christians, and it alone sets the heart at liberty.
magis: Catechism 1741
By his glorious Cross Christ has won salvation for all and redeemed us from the sin that held us in bondage; for freedom Christ has set us free.
Catechism 1814–1815
Faith is the virtue by which we believe in God and all that he has revealed; faith without hope and love does not fully unite the believer to Christ and does not make him a living member of his Body.
Catechism 1972
The New Law is a law of love, a law of grace and a law of freedom, which makes us act out of love rather than fear.
Catechism 1504
Jesus often makes use of signs to heal, such as spittle and the laying on of hands; in the sacraments Christ continues to touch us in order to heal us.

The Latin Church keeps the Annunciation of the Lord on Monday 5 April this year (moved from 25 March, which fell on Pesaha Thursday); Syro-Malabar faithful follow the direction of their eparchy.
2027-04-07.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen Saviour, you won our freedom, and you opened the ears of the deaf and loosed the tongue of the mute. Say over us your word, Ephphatha: open our ears to hear your Gospel and our lips to proclaim your praise. Keep us from every yoke of slavery, and let our faith be faith working through love, so that all may say of your work in us, He has done everything well. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-04-08.title: Second Thursday of Resurrection
2027-04-08.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The privilege of believing in Christ and suffering for him
The faith of the Canaanite woman
2027-04-08.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost.
2027-04-08.verse: Then Jesus answered her, “Woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you wish.” And her daughter was healed instantly.
theo: Paul writes to the Philippians from prison, not knowing whether he will live or die. He does not ask them to get him released. He asks for something harder: “Only, live your life in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ.” The Greek word Paul uses means to live as a citizen; Philippi was a Roman colony, proud of its citizenship, and Paul tells them that they belong to a greater city, and must live by its laws. A Christian's daily conduct is the visible face of the Gospel. Paul hopes to hear “that you are standing firm in one spirit, striving side by side with one mind for the faith of the gospel, and are in no way intimidated by your opponents.” Then he says something no one could invent: “For he has graciously granted you the privilege not only of believing in Christ, but of suffering for him as well.” Suffering for Christ is called a gift of grace, a privilege, like faith itself. The apostles in Jerusalem had understood this when, after being flogged, “they rejoiced that they were considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the sake of the name” (Acts 5:41). Easter does not remove the Cross from the Christian life; it changes its meaning. Those who suffer with the Risen Lord share his victory.

In the Gospel Jesus goes north into the district of Tyre and Sidon, outside the land of Israel. A woman comes out to meet him, and Matthew calls her a Canaanite, using the oldest name for the peoples who lived in the land before Israel: she is as much an outsider as anyone could be. Yet her first words are a confession of faith: “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David; my daughter is tormented by a demon.” What follows is one of the hardest scenes in the Gospels. “But he did not answer her at all.” The disciples want her sent away. Jesus says he was sent “only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” She will not go. “But she came and knelt before him, saying, ‘Lord, help me.’” Three words, one of the shortest prayers in the Bible and perhaps the most prayed. Jesus answers with a proverb that sounds harsh: “It is not fair to take the children's food and throw it to the dogs.” And she, with a mother's courage and quick wit, turns his own words into her plea: “Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters' table.”

“Then Jesus answered her, ‘Woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you wish.’ And her daughter was healed instantly.” Only twice in Matthew's Gospel does Jesus single out someone's faith for such praise, and both times the person is a Gentile: the centurion at Capernaum and this Canaanite mother. The silence and the hard words were not rejection; they drew out of her a faith that grew stronger with every refusal. The Fathers saw in her the whole Gentile world, waiting at the edge of Israel's table for the bread of life, and receiving not crumbs but the whole loaf. After the Resurrection the Lord will send his apostles to “make disciples of all nations” (Matthew 28:19); the Gospel came to India with Saint Thomas, and the Church of the Saint Thomas Christians is one of the fruits of that mission. Every Holy Qurbana is that table: the children's bread is now given to all who come in faith. And every mother who has prayed for years for a sick or wandering child can stand beside this woman. God's silence is not his absence. Keep kneeling; keep saying, Lord, help me.
conn: Rejoicing to suffer.
“They rejoiced that they were considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the sake of the name” (Acts 5:41); “Blessed are you when people revile you and persecute you” (Matthew 5:11).
Citizens of heaven.
“But our citizenship is in heaven, and it is from there that we are expecting a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ” (Philippians 3:20).
Be strong and courageous.
“Be strong and courageous; do not be frightened or dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go” (Joshua 1:9).
A foreigner's faith.
Ruth the Moabite says, “your people shall be my people, and your God my God” (Ruth 1:16); she became an ancestor of David and of Christ (Matthew 1:5).
Great faith in a Gentile.
Jesus says of the centurion, “in no one in Israel have I found such faith” (Matthew 8:10).
All nations.
The Risen Lord sends the eleven: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations” (Matthew 28:19).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana we are all given the children's bread: not crumbs from the table but the Body and Blood of the Lord himself, given to all who come in faith and humility.
Before Holy Communion we pray in our own words what the Canaanite mother prayed: we are not worthy, yet we trust in his mercy. Lord, help me.
outline: Opening
A prisoner who asks not for release but for a worthy life.
Point 1 · Worthy of the gospel
Citizens of a greater city.
Point 2 · The privilege of suffering
The Cross after Easter.
Point 3 · Lord, help me
Silence, refusal and a mother who will not leave.
Point 4 · Great is your faith
Children's bread for all the nations.
Closing image
A mother kneeling at the back of a church, night after night, for her child.
Take-home line
“Lord, help me.”
live: Live worthily (Philippians 1:27)
Choose one area of daily conduct, at work or online, where your behaviour does not yet match the Gospel, and change it.
Offer a suffering
Unite one pain or humiliation this week to the Cross of Christ, and offer it for someone.
Pray one of the shortest prayers (Matthew 15:25)
Whenever you are anxious this week, say: Lord, help me.
Pray for a child
Pray daily this week for a child, your own or another's, who is sick or far from God.
fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)

To suffer for Christ is a greater gift than to raise the dead or to work miracles. When I work a miracle I am in debt to Christ; when I suffer for Christ, he counts himself in my debt. That is why Paul calls suffering a grace that has been given to you.
St Augustine (in substance)

She did not take offence when she was called a dog. She said, Yes, Lord. By humbly accepting what she was, she was made what she was not: from a dog she became a daughter. Humility opened the door that pride would have shut.
magis: Catechism 2616
Jesus already answers prayer during his ministry, hearing the prayer of faith expressed in words, as with the leper, Jairus, the Canaanite woman and the good thief.
Catechism 543
Everyone is called to enter the Kingdom; first announced to the children of Israel, it is meant to welcome people of all nations.
Catechism 618
The Cross is the unique sacrifice of Christ, yet he calls his disciples to take up their cross and follow him, associating them with his redeeming sacrifice.
Catechism 2473
Martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith; the martyr bears witness to Christ who died and rose.
saints: This week

Monday 5 to Saturday 10 April: the second week of the Resurrection. Sunday 11 April: the Third Sunday of Resurrection. The Latin Church keeps the Annunciation of the Lord on Monday 5 April this year (moved from 25 March, which fell on Pesaha Thursday); Syro-Malabar faithful follow the direction of their eparchy.
2027-04-08.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of David, risen Saviour of all nations, you heard the cry of the Canaanite mother and praised her great faith. Have mercy on us, and help us. Give us her humility and her perseverance, so that we do not give up when you seem silent. Make us live in a manner worthy of your Gospel, standing firm together and unafraid, and count it a grace to suffer for your name. Feed us at your table with the bread of your children, and send us to all who wait for it. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-04-09.title: Second Friday of Resurrection
2027-04-09.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-04-09.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost. On Fridays the Church remembers the Passion of the Lord; in the Easter season it remembers it in the light of the Resurrection.
2027-04-09.verse: For the message about the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.
theo: Every Friday is a little Good Friday, and on this Friday of the Easter season Paul brings us back to the Cross. Corinth was a city that admired clever speakers and new ideas. Into that world Paul brought a message that sounded absurd: that the Saviour of the world was a man executed on a Roman cross, the death reserved for slaves and rebels. “For the message about the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.” Paul does not soften the scandal. He quotes Isaiah: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart.” Then he asks: “Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?” Human wisdom, for all its brilliance, did not find its way to God. So “God decided, through the foolishness of our proclamation, to save those who believe.” The Cross is not a clever argument that wins debates; it is an act of love that saves. After Easter we know that the Crucified is alive, and that is why the Cross is the power of God: the weakest moment in history became the moment death was defeated.

Paul describes the two ways people resist this message. Some want signs, proofs of power; others want wisdom, a philosophy that satisfies the mind. “But we proclaim Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, but to those who are the called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.” Paul himself was a Jew, and the first to receive this message in Jerusalem were Jews; he is describing not a people but a temptation found in every human heart, which wants God to prove himself on our terms. Our own age asks for both: give us miracles on demand, give us arguments we can control. God gives instead a crucified and risen Lord. The Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala have long venerated the Cross without the figure of the Body, the Cross of the Resurrection, glorious because the Lord is risen; the Mar Thoma Cross with its flowering arms and the dove above shows the tree of death become the tree of life. The Cross is not the end of Christ's story but the door to Easter.

In the Gospel Jesus sits in a boat and teaches the crowd on the shore. “Listen! A sower went out to sow.” The seed falls on four kinds of ground: the hard path where birds snatch it, the rocky ground where it springs up and withers, the thorns that choke it, and the good soil where it yields “thirty and sixty and a hundredfold.” Jesus himself is the sower, and his word is the seed. The parable is honest: much of the sowing seems wasted. Yet the sower keeps sowing, generously, even on the path, because the harvest in the good soil is beyond all calculation. The two readings belong together. The Cross itself looked like seed thrown away: a life buried in the ground. Jesus said, “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). Easter is that harvest. The question the parable leaves with us is not about the sower but about the soil: what kind of ground does the word find in me? “Let anyone with ears to hear listen!”
conn: The wisdom of the wise.
Paul quotes Isaiah 29:14: “The wisdom of their wise shall perish, and the discernment of the discerning shall be hidden.”
Him crucified.
“For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2).
The Servant's wounds.
“But he was wounded for our transgressions… and by his bruises we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5).
The word that does not return empty.
“So shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty” (Isaiah 55:11).
The grain of wheat.
“Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24).
Patient endurance.
In Luke the good soil are those who “hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patient endurance” (Luke 8:15).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the one sacrifice of the Cross is made present, not repeated: the Lord who was crucified offers himself to the Father, and the Risen Lord gives himself to us as food.
The word sown in the readings and the Bread broken at the altar are one gift: the seed that died and rose, now bearing fruit in those who receive him.
outline: Opening
Every Friday is a little Good Friday, even in Easter.
Point 1 · The message about the cross
Foolishness and the power of God.
Point 2 · Christ crucified
Not signs on demand, not wisdom we control.
Point 3 · A sower went out to sow
Generous seed on every kind of ground.
Point 4 · Thirty, sixty, a hundredfold
The grain that dies and the Easter harvest.
Closing image
The Mar Thoma Cross, flowering at its ends.
Take-home line
“To us who are being saved it is the power of God.”
live: Look at the Cross (1 Corinthians 1:18)
Spend five minutes today before a crucifix or the Mar Thoma Cross and thank the Lord for his love.
Clear the ground (Mark 4:7)
Name one ‘thorn’ that chokes God's word in you, such as worry or a screen habit, and cut it back this week.
Sow generously
Share a Gospel verse with someone this week, without worrying about the result.
Read slowly
Read Mark 4:1–20 at home and ask which ground you are today.
fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)

The Cross won the world, and through unlearned men. Fishermen and tentmakers persuaded philosophers and kings; men without eloquence overcame the orators. This is the clearest sign that the Cross is the power of God: it did not need human wisdom, and it conquered all of it.
St Gregory the Great (in substance)

The good soil brings forth fruit through patience. Whatever good we do is nothing unless we bear patiently the evils done to us by our neighbour. The seed that falls in the good earth must endure the winter before it rises in the harvest.
magis: Catechism 272

Faith in God's almighty power is put to the test by evil and suffering; but in the Resurrection of Christ, God has shown the immeasurable greatness of his power: Christ crucified is the power of God and the wisdom of God.
Catechism 616
It is love to the end that gives Christ's sacrifice its value as redemption and reparation.
Catechism 543
The word of the Lord is compared to a seed sown in a field; those who hear it with faith and join the little flock of Christ have welcomed the Kingdom.
Catechism 2653
The Church urges all the faithful to learn the surpassing knowledge of Jesus Christ by frequent reading of the divine Scriptures, accompanied by prayer.
saints: This week

Monday 5 to Saturday 10 April: the second week of the Resurrection. Sunday 11 April: the Third Sunday of Resurrection. The Latin Church keeps the Annunciation of the Lord on Monday 5 April this year (moved from 25 March, which fell on Pesaha Thursday); Syro-Malabar faithful follow the direction of their eparchy.
2027-04-09.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, crucified and risen, the message of your Cross is foolishness to the world but to us the power of God. Keep us from demanding signs on our own terms and from trusting only our own wisdom. You are the sower who goes out to sow: make our hearts good soil, clear away the stones and thorns, and let your word bear fruit in us, thirty, sixty and a hundredfold. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-04-10.title: Second Saturday of Resurrection
2027-04-10.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts
2027-04-10.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost.
2027-04-10.verse: Look at my hands and my feet; see that it is I myself. Touch me and see; for a ghost does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.
theo: Paul's letter to the Colossians describes the new life of those who have been raised with Christ in Baptism. Just before today's passage he tells them to put on, like new clothes, “compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience,” and to forgive one another as the Lord has forgiven them. Then comes the garment that holds all the others together: “Above all, clothe yourselves with love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony.” Love is the belt that keeps the other virtues from falling off. Then Paul gives three gifts for a Christian home and community. The first: “let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in the one body. And be thankful.” The word ‘rule’ is the word for an umpire in the games: when we are pulled in different directions, the peace of Christ is to make the call. The second: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly.” Not visit occasionally, but dwell, live in the house, have its own room. The third: “with gratitude in your hearts sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs to God.” A Christian family that prays together, reads the Gospel together and sings together is a small church. Kerala Christian homes have long kept this at dusk, when the lamp is lit and the family gathers for evening prayer: that moment is Colossians 3 lived out. Saturday is also the day the Church honours the Blessed Virgin Mary, who kept all the words of her Son and pondered them in her heart (Luke 2:19): she is the model of the word of Christ dwelling richly in a home.

Paul ends with a rule that covers all of life: “And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.” There is nothing too ordinary to be done in the name of Jesus: cooking, studying, driving, nursing, ploughing. And everything is to be done with thanksgiving. The Greek word for giving thanks is the root of the word Eucharist; the Syriac word Qurbana means the offering. A Christian life is meant to become one long Qurbana: an offering of everything to the Father, through the Son, with thanks.

In the Gospel we are back on Easter evening in Jerusalem. The two disciples from Emmaus are telling their story when “Jesus himself stood among them and said to them, ‘Peace be with you.’” The disciples were terrified: “They were startled and terrified, and thought that they were seeing a ghost.” Jesus answers with a tenderness that is almost humorous: “Why are you frightened, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? Look at my hands and my feet; see that it is I myself. Touch me and see; for a ghost does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.” Then, because they are still disbelieving for joy, he asks, “Have you anything here to eat?” “They gave him a piece of broiled fish, and he took it and ate in their presence.” Luke insists on the body because the faith of the Church depends on it. The Resurrection is not a beautiful idea, a memory, or a vision; the One who was crucified is alive in his own body, glorified and no longer subject to death, yet the same body that bears the wounds. That is why Christians bury their dead with reverence and wait for the resurrection of the body. And the One who ate fish with his friends gives himself to us as food at every Holy Qurbana: his true Body and Blood, risen and living.
conn: Clothed with Christ.
“As many of you as were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ” (Galatians 3:27).
Love above all.
“Many waters cannot quench love, neither can floods drown it” (Song of Songs 8:7); “the greatest of these is love” (1 Corinthians 13:13).
The peace of the Lord.
The priestly blessing: “the LORD lift up his countenance upon you, and give you peace” (Numbers 6:26); Jesus' first word on Easter evening is “Peace be with you” (Luke 24:36).
Singing to God.
“O sing to the LORD a new song; sing to the LORD, all the earth” (Psalm 96:1); “be filled with the Spirit… singing and making melody to the Lord in your hearts” (Ephesians 5:18–19).
In my flesh I shall see God.
Job's hope: “then in my flesh I shall see God” (Job 19:26).
Ate and drank with him.
Peter tells Cornelius that the apostles are witnesses “who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead” (Acts 10:41); John: “what we have looked at and touched with our hands” (1 John 1:1).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Risen Lord stands among us and says, Peace be with you. He gives us not a memory but himself, his glorified Body and Blood, truly present.
The whole Qurbana is thanksgiving: everything we have done in word and deed during the week is brought to the altar and offered to the Father through the Son.
outline: Opening
The lamp lit at dusk and the family gathered to pray.
Point 1 · Above all, love
The belt that holds the virtues together.
Point 2 · The peace of Christ rule
The umpire in our hearts.
Point 3 · The word dwelling richly, with songs
The home as a little church.
Point 4 · Touch me and see
The real body of the Risen Lord.
Closing image
A piece of broiled fish on a plate in an upper room.
Take-home line
“See that it is I myself.”
live: Keep evening prayer (Colossians 3:16)
Gather the family for prayer every evening this week, light the lamp, read a few lines of the Gospel and sing one hymn.
Let peace decide (Colossians 3:15)
Before an important decision this week, ask: what keeps the peace of Christ in my heart?
Do it in his name (Colossians 3:17)
Begin your work each morning with the sign of the cross and a short thanksgiving.
Honour the body
Visit the grave of a family member and pray for them, in hope of the resurrection of the body.
fathers: St Ignatius of Antioch (in substance)

I know and believe that he was in the flesh even after the Resurrection. When he came to Peter and those with him, he said, Take hold of me, touch me and see that I am not a spirit without a body. They touched him at once and believed. After his Resurrection he ate and drank with them as one who has flesh, though he was spiritually one with the Father.
St Augustine (in substance)
Singing belongs to the one who loves. The new song is sung by the new man, who has been made new by love; let your life sing, so that your voice does not sing alone.
magis: Catechism 645

The Risen Jesus establishes direct contact with his disciples through touch and the sharing of a meal; his body is the same body that was crucified, bearing the marks of his Passion, yet now with new properties of a glorious body.
Catechism 999
Christ is raised with his own body: ‘See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself’; so in him all will rise again with their own bodies.
Catechism 1360
The Eucharist is a sacrifice of thanksgiving to the Father, a blessing by which the Church expresses her gratitude to God for all his benefits.
Catechism 1156–1158
Song and music are woven into the liturgy; they express prayer more beautifully, unite the assembly and give greater solemnity to the rites.
Catechism 2204–2205
The Christian family is a communion of persons and can and should be called a domestic church, a community of faith, hope and charity.
saints: This week

Monday 5 to Saturday 10 April: the second week of the Resurrection. Sunday 11 April: the Third Sunday of Resurrection. The Latin Church keeps the Annunciation of the Lord on Monday 5 April this year (moved from 25 March, which fell on Pesaha Thursday); Syro-Malabar faithful follow the direction of their eparchy.
2027-04-10.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you stood among your frightened disciples and said, Peace be with you; you showed them your hands and your feet and ate before them. Strengthen our faith in your true Resurrection and in the resurrection of the body. Clothe us with love above all, let your peace rule in our hearts, and let your word dwell in our homes richly, so that with grateful hearts we may sing to the Father and do everything in your name. With the Blessed Virgin Mary, who kept your words in her heart, we praise you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-04-12.title: Third Monday of Resurrection
2027-04-12.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Be patient until the coming of the Lord
2027-04-12.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). Third week of the Resurrection. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and “Queen of Heaven” is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost.
2027-04-12.verse: Keep awake therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour.
theo: James writes to poor Christians, many of them labourers who waited at the end of the day for wages that did not always come. He does not tell them to stop waiting; he teaches them how to wait. “Be patient, therefore, beloved, until the coming of the Lord. The farmer waits for the precious crop from the earth, being patient with it until it receives the early and the late rains.” Every farmer in Kerala knows this patience. He ploughs and sows, and then he can only look at the sky and wait for the rains of June and the rains of October; no amount of worry will bring a cloud one day sooner. Yet his waiting is not idle. He mends the bunds, he weeds, he watches. That is the waiting of a Christian in the Easter season. The Lord is risen; he has ascended to the Father; he will come again in glory. Between his rising and his return we live like farmers between sowing and harvest. “You also must be patient. Strengthen your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is near.” James then names the sin that grows quickly among people who are tired of waiting: “Beloved, do not grumble against one another, so that you may not be judged. See, the Judge is standing at the doors!” When we are anxious, we turn on each other. He points instead to the prophets and to Job, who suffered without letting go of God, and to what Job discovered at the end: “how the Lord is compassionate and merciful.” Finally, a short word about speech: “let your ‘Yes’ be yes and your ‘No’ be no.” A person who lives before the coming Lord does not need oaths to be believed; his plain word is enough.

The Gospel tells the same truth in the language of a village wedding. In the custom of the time the bridegroom came, often late at night, to bring his bride to his father's house, and young women went out with lamps to light the procession and enter the feast with him. “Ten bridesmaids took their lamps and went to meet the bridegroom. Five of them were foolish, and five were wise.” Notice what is not different between them. All ten were invited, all ten had lamps, all ten were waiting, and all ten fell asleep: “As the bridegroom was delayed, all of them became drowsy and slept.” The difference is the oil. “When the foolish took their lamps, they took no oil with them; but the wise took flasks of oil with their lamps.” Then the cry at midnight: “Look! Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him.” The foolish ask to borrow, and they are refused, not out of meanness but because some things cannot be lent. No one can lend me his faith, his love or his years of prayer at the last minute; the oil must be my own. The ending is the most serious line of the parable: “and the door was shut.” This is not a story to frighten us but to wake us up. In the Easter season the Church hears it with new ears. The Bridegroom who was “taken away” on Good Friday (Matthew 9:15) has come back from the grave, and the wedding feast has already begun at every altar. Our lamp was lit at Baptism, from the light of the Risen Christ. The oil that keeps it burning is charity, daily prayer, the Holy Qurbana and confession. In many Kerala homes a lamp is still lit at dusk and the family gathers before it to pray; the parable asks whether the lamp of the heart is burning as faithfully as the lamp in the front room.

James and Matthew fit together. The farmer waits with patience and keeps working; the wise bridesmaids sleep, but they are ready when the cry comes. Christian waiting is neither panic nor laziness. It is the calm readiness of people who know that the One who is coming is not a stranger but the Bridegroom who loves them, the Risen Lord who has already shown them his hands and his side. “Keep awake therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour.” That is not a threat to those who love him; it is an invitation to live every ordinary day as a day on which he might knock.
outline: Opening
A farmer watching the sky after sowing, and a lamp lit at dusk in a Kerala home.
Point 1 · The patience of the farmer
Strengthen your hearts; do not grumble; let your yes be yes.
Point 2 · Lamps without oil
All ten slept; only five were ready.
Point 3 · Here is the bridegroom
The Risen Lord is coming; the feast has begun.
Take-home line
“Keep awake therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour.”
live: Strengthen your heart (James 5:8)
When you feel the urge to grumble against someone at home or at work today, stop and say a short prayer for that person instead.
Buy oil while there is time (Matthew 25:4)
Choose one daily practice that keeps your lamp burning, such as the evening family prayer before the lamp, and keep it every day this week.
2027-04-12.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Bridegroom of the Church, you rose from the dead and you will come again in glory. Give us the patience of the farmer who waits for the rain, and the readiness of the wise who kept oil in their lamps. Keep us from grumbling against one another, make our yes a true yes, and let the light lit in us at Baptism burn with love until the cry is heard at midnight and we go in with you to the wedding feast. Amen. Alleluia!
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the wedding feast of the Lamb has already begun. The Bridegroom comes to his bride, the Church, under the signs of bread and wine, and each Communion is a foretaste of the day when the door opens and we enter with him for ever.

2027-04-13.title: Third Tuesday of Resurrection
2027-04-13.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-04-13.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). Third week of the Resurrection.
2027-04-13.verse: Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.
theo: The First Letter to the Thessalonians is probably the oldest Christian writing we possess, written only about twenty years after the Resurrection to a community that was a few months old. Paul had been forced to leave the city quickly, and he writes like a father who could not finish teaching his children. At the end of the letter he gathers his advice into a string of short commands, almost like a rule of life for a new parish. He begins with those who serve: “But we appeal to you, brothers and sisters, to respect those who labor among you, and have charge of you in the Lord and admonish you; esteem them very highly in love because of their work. Be at peace among yourselves.” A parish lives by the labour of many people: the priest, the sisters, the catechism teachers who come every Sunday morning, the sacristan who opens the church before dawn, the choir, the family units. Paul asks that they be held in love, not because they are perfect but “because of their work.” Then he turns to the care of the weak: “admonish the idlers, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with all of them. See that none of you repays evil for evil, but always seek to do good to one another and to all.” Each kind of person needs a different kind of love: a word of correction for one, a word of courage for another, a hand for a third, and patience for everyone.

Then come three short lines that sum up the Easter life: “Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.” Paul is not asking us to feel cheerful all the time. He wrote these words to a persecuted church. Christian joy rests not on our circumstances but on the fact that Christ is risen, and that fact does not change when the day goes badly. Prayer without ceasing is not endless words but a heart turned toward God all day, returning to him again and again, the way a mother's heart keeps returning to a sick child. Thanksgiving in all circumstances is the language of the Holy Qurbana, whose very name in Greek, Eucharist, means thanksgiving. Then Paul looks toward the gift of Pentecost: “Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise the words of prophets, but test everything; hold fast to what is good; abstain from every form of evil.” The Spirit is like a fire that can be smothered by neglect or by fear. A Christian is open to the Spirit, yet not naive: he tests, he weighs things by the faith of the Church, he holds on to the good and lets the evil go.

In the Gospel Jesus explains the parable of the sower to his disciples. “The sower sows the word.” The seed is always good; the difference lies in the soil. On the path, the word never goes in: “Satan immediately comes and takes away the word that is sown in them.” On rocky ground, the word is welcomed “with joy”, but it has no root, and when trouble comes, “immediately they fall away.” Among thorns, the word grows for a while, but “the cares of the world, and the lure of wealth, and the desire for other things come in and choke the word, and it yields nothing.” Finally the good soil: “they hear the word and accept it and bear fruit, thirty and sixty and a hundredfold.” The Easter season is a time of harvest and of testing. Many people came to the Easter Qurbana with joy. Will that joy put down roots, or will it wither with the first difficulty? Will the worries of exams, loans and prices, and the pull of money and pleasure, choke what grew at Easter? The parable is not a sorting of people into fixed groups. Each of us has some path, some rock and some thorns in the heart. The Lord gives us the readings of this day as a farmer's tools: patient prayer breaks up the hard path, perseverance in trial lets roots go down, and thanksgiving pulls out the thorns of anxiety.
outline: Opening
Ask: who are the people who labour among us in this parish?
Point 1 · Esteem them very highly in love
Respect, correction, courage, help and patience.
Point 2 · Rejoice, pray, give thanks
The Easter life in three lines; do not quench the Spirit.
Point 3 · The sower sows the word
Path, rock, thorns and good soil in one heart.
Take-home line
“Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances.”
live: Thank one who labours (1 Thessalonians 5:12)
Thank your vicar, a catechism teacher or the sacristan this week, in person or with a short note.
Pull out one thorn (Mark 4:19)
Name one worry or desire that is choking your prayer, and hand it to the Lord each morning this week.
2027-04-13.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen Sower of the word, you scatter your seed generously on every heart. Break up the hard paths in us, give our joy deep roots, and pull out the thorns of worry and greed. Teach us to rejoice always, to pray without ceasing and to give thanks in all circumstances. Let us not quench your Spirit, but hold fast to what is good, so that your word may bear fruit in us thirty and sixty and a hundredfold. Amen. Alleluia!
altar: The Holy Qurbana is the great thanksgiving that Paul asks for: in every circumstance the Church lifts up the Body and Blood of the Risen Christ and gives thanks to the Father. Here, too, the Sower sows the word in the readings before he gives himself as the Bread of life.

2027-04-14.title: Third Wednesday of Resurrection
2027-04-14.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: To me, living is Christ and dying is gain
2027-04-14.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). Third week of the Resurrection.
2027-04-14.verse: For to me, living is Christ and dying is gain.
theo: Paul writes to the Philippians from prison, not knowing whether his trial will end in release or in death. A man in that position might be expected to write about his fear. Instead he writes one of the most serene sentences in the New Testament: “For to me, living is Christ and dying is gain.” Everything turns on the first half. If living were money, then dying would be loss; if living were reputation, success or pleasure, death would take it all away. But if living is Christ, then death cannot take away what matters, because it brings us closer to him. That is why Paul can weigh the two possibilities so calmly. “If I am to live in the flesh, that means fruitful labor for me; and I do not know which I prefer. I am hard pressed between the two: my desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better; but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for you.” This is Easter faith in its plainest form. Because Christ has been raised, death has lost its sting (1 Corinthians 15:55). Paul does not despise this life. He loves the Philippians and wants to stay with them “for your progress and joy in faith.” But he has stopped being afraid of the end. For him, to die is to “be with Christ”, and to live is to serve him in his brothers and sisters. A Christian who has learned this can face illness, old age, danger and even martyrdom with a peace that the world cannot explain. The Church in India has seen this peace in her martyrs and in many ordinary believers who died with the name of Jesus on their lips. When we pray the Office for the departed at a funeral, we are not pretending that death does not hurt. We are saying, with Paul, that for those who belong to Christ it is the door to something far better.

Matthew places the cleansing of a leper immediately after the Sermon on the Mount, as if to say: here is the teacher who spoke with such authority; now see what his authority does. “When Jesus had come down from the mountain, great crowds followed him; and there was a leper who came to him and knelt before him, saying, ‘Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.’” Under the Law of Moses a person with a leprous disease had to live apart: “He shall live alone; his dwelling shall be outside the camp” (Leviticus 13:46). The rule protected the community, but it meant years of loneliness, and the leper should not even have come near. He does not doubt that Jesus can heal him; his only question is whether Jesus wants to. Jesus answers with his hand before his words: “He stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, ‘I do choose. Be made clean!’ Immediately his leprosy was cleansed.” The touch that should have made Jesus unclean makes the leper clean. Holiness here is not something fragile that must be protected from contact; it is a power that flows outward and heals. Then Jesus sends him to the priest, “and offer the gift that Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.” Jesus does not set the Law aside; he fulfils it, and he gives the man back not only his skin but his place in the worshipping community of Israel. The Risen Lord still stretches out his hand. In the sacrament of Reconciliation he touches what we are ashamed to show anyone, and says, I do choose. In the Anointing of the Sick he lays his hand on the suffering. And at every Qurbana, before Communion, we pray in humility because we know we need his touch.
outline: Opening
A prisoner who is not afraid, and a leper who dares to come near.
Point 1 · Living is Christ
If he is my life, death cannot rob me.
Point 2 · Far better, yet more necessary
Paul torn between heaven and his people.
Point 3 · I do choose
The touch that makes clean and restores to the community.
Take-home line
“For to me, living is Christ and dying is gain.”
live: Ask what your life is (Philippians 1:21)
Finish the sentence honestly today: “For me, living is …”. Then ask the Lord to make the answer Christ.
Touch someone who is shunned (Matthew 8:3)
Visit, call or sit beside someone who is avoided because of illness, age, disgrace or poverty.
2027-04-14.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you are our life, and in you death becomes gain. Deliver us from the fear of death and from every false life that cannot last. Make us love the people you have given us and serve them gladly while we remain here. Stretch out your hand to us as you did to the leper; touch the places we hide, and say to each of us, I do choose. Be made clean. Amen. Alleluia!
altar: The hand that touched the leper is the hand that took bread and gave thanks. In the Holy Qurbana the Risen Lord touches us with his own Body, and we, who are not worthy, are made clean and gathered again into his people.

2027-04-15.title: Third Thursday of Resurrection
2027-04-15.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-04-15.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). Third week of the Resurrection.
2027-04-15.verse: He woke up and rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” Then the wind ceased, and there was a dead calm.
theo: Paul spent years organising a collection among his Gentile churches for the poor Christians of Jerusalem. It was more than relief work. For Paul it was a sign that the Church is one body, that the nations who had received the gospel from Jerusalem now shared their goods with the mother Church. Here he holds up an unexpected example to the wealthy Corinthians: the churches of Macedonia, who were themselves poor and persecuted. “For during a severe ordeal of affliction, their abundant joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part.” Joy and poverty together produced generosity: that is the arithmetic of grace. They gave “according to their means, and even beyond their means,” and they begged Paul for “the privilege of sharing in this ministry to the saints.” Then he gives the secret: “they gave themselves first to the Lord.” Generosity with money follows the gift of oneself, never the other way round. Older Kerala Christians remember the custom of the handful of rice, the pidiyari: each day the mother of the house set aside a fistful of rice from the family's portion for the church and the poor, even in years of want. It was the Macedonian spirit in a Kerala kitchen. Paul then lifts the whole matter to the level of Christ: “For you know the generous act of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich.” The Son of God emptied himself into our poverty, even the poverty of the tomb, so that we might share the riches of his Resurrection. Every Christian act of giving is a small echo of that great exchange. Finally Paul gently presses the Corinthians, who had made a good start a year before: “now finish doing it.” Good intentions are not yet generosity.

In the Gospel, evening has come after a long day of teaching by the lake. Jesus says, “Let us go across to the other side,” toward the Gentile shore. “A great windstorm arose, and the waves beat into the boat, so that the boat was already being swamped. But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion.” The disciples are experienced fishermen, and they are terrified. Their cry is half prayer and half accusation: “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?” It is a cry many believers have made in illness, debt, grief or persecution. Jesus gets up and speaks to the storm as one speaks to a disobedient servant: “Peace! Be still!” and there is “a dead calm.” Then he turns to them: “Why are you afraid? Have you still no faith?” The Psalms had said that only the LORD rules the raging sea: “he made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed” (Psalm 107:29). So the disciples' final question answers itself: “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” The early Church read this scene in the light of Easter. The Lord who slept in the boat is the Lord who slept in the tomb, and the one who rose up to calm the sea is the one who rose from the dead to calm the fear of his disciples. The boat is the Church, crossing to the other side with Christ on board, through every storm of history. He may seem to be asleep; he is never absent. St Augustine used to say, in substance, that when a storm rises in us, of anger or fear or temptation, it is because Christ is asleep in us, that is, our faith in him has fallen asleep: wake him by remembering him, and there will be calm. Kerala knows both storms and boats. In the floods of August 2018, fishermen from the coast carried their own boats inland and rescued thousands of strangers. In the storm of fear, the Risen Lord asks us to be that kind of people: not paralysed, but generous, steady, and sure that he is with us.

The two readings belong together. Fear makes us cling to what we have; faith opens our hands to give. The Macedonians were in a storm of affliction, and still they gave with joy, because they had first given themselves to the Lord who is master of the storm. When we trust that Christ is in the boat, we can afford to be generous.
outline: Opening
A mother setting aside a handful of rice, and fishermen in a sinking boat.
Point 1 · Joy and poverty overflowed
The Macedonians gave themselves first to the Lord.
Point 2 · Rich, yet he became poor
The great exchange; now finish what you began.
Point 3 · Peace! Be still!
The Lord in the stern of the Church's boat.
Take-home line
“Why are you afraid? Have you still no faith?”
live: A handful for the poor (2 Corinthians 8:3)
Set aside something small every day this week, money or rice, for the poor or for the parish charity box.
Wake him up (Mark 4:38)
When fear or anger rises in you today, stop and say slowly: Jesus, you are in my boat.
2027-04-15.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, though you were rich, for our sake you became poor, so that by your poverty we might become rich. Teach us the joy of the Macedonians, who gave themselves first to you and then gave beyond their means. When storms rise around us and within us, and you seem to be asleep, help us to call on you with faith. Speak your word, Peace! Be still!, over our fears, and make us generous and calm because you are with us in the boat. Amen. Alleluia!
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Lord who became poor for us gives himself completely under the humble signs of bread and wine. In the offering of the gifts we bring our own small gifts, and we learn from him to give ourselves first.

2027-04-16.title: Third Friday of Resurrection
2027-04-16.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Please your neighbour for his good
2027-04-16.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). Third week of the Resurrection.
2027-04-16.verse: After looking around at all of them, he said to him, “Stretch out your hand.” He did so, and his hand was restored.
theo: The Christians of Rome were divided. Some felt at liberty to eat any food; others, with a more anxious conscience, kept to vegetables and observed special days. Each group was tempted to despise or judge the other. Paul, who counts himself among the “strong”, does not tell the strong that they are wrong in their freedom. He tells them what love does with freedom: “We who are strong ought to put up with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Each of us must please our neighbor for the good purpose of building up the neighbor.” The test of any Christian freedom is whether it builds others up. Then Paul gives the reason, and it is Christ himself: “For Christ did not please himself; but, as it is written, ‘The insults of those who insult you have fallen on me.’” He quotes a psalm of the suffering righteous one (Psalm 69:9). Jesus could have pleased himself; instead he carried the insults meant for others, all the way to the Cross. On a Friday the Church remembers that Cross, and in the Easter season she sees it as the tree of life. To bear with the weakness of a brother or sister is to stand a little under that Cross. Paul then says something precious about the Bible: “For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, so that by steadfastness and by the encouragement of the scriptures we might have hope.” The Scriptures are not a museum of old stories; they are a daily source of steadfastness and comfort. And he ends with a prayer that every family, every parish and every Church needs: “May the God of steadfastness and encouragement grant you to live in harmony with one another, in accordance with Christ Jesus, so that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Where disagreements, even about holy things, have wounded us, Paul does not ask us to pretend there is no difference. He asks us to bear with one another, to seek what builds up, and to let our praise become one voice again.

In the Gospel Jesus enters a synagogue on the sabbath to teach. “There was a man there whose right hand was withered.” Luke, a careful observer, notes that it was the right hand, the hand with which a man worked and earned his bread. “The scribes and the Pharisees watched him to see whether he would cure on the sabbath, so that they might find an accusation against him.” The sabbath was God's gift to Israel, a holy day of rest and freedom, and Jewish teachers themselves held that saving a life sets aside the sabbath rest. The question here was whether a healing that could wait until the next day should be done on the holy day. Jesus does not argue in secret. He says to the man, “Come and stand here,” and brings him into the middle, where everyone must look at him. Then he turns the question back to them: “I ask you, is it lawful to do good or to do harm on the sabbath, to save life or to destroy it?” For Jesus, the sabbath is not a day when love must wait. It is the day that most belongs to God, and so it is the day most fit for the works of God. “After looking around at all of them, he said to him, ‘Stretch out your hand.’ He did so, and his hand was restored.” The man had to do something: he had to stretch out the very hand that could not move. Faith often begins like that, with obeying a word that seems impossible. Some of those present “were filled with fury”.
