The Gospel does not ask us to blame them, but to examine ourselves, because religious people of every age can love their rules more than the person in front of them. Christians keep Sunday, the first day of the week and the day of the Resurrection, as the Lord's Day. We keep it holy above all in the Holy Qurbana, and then in rest, in family, and in works of mercy: visiting the sick, helping the poor, reconciling with an enemy. The Risen Lord still says to every withered life: Stretch out your hand.
outline: Opening
A man with a withered right hand in the middle of the synagogue.
Point 1 · Not to please ourselves
The strong bear with the weak, as Christ bore our insults.
Point 2 · With one voice
The Scriptures give hope; God grants harmony.
Point 3 · Stretch out your hand
The sabbath, the Lord's Day, and the works of God.
Take-home line
“Is it lawful to do good or to do harm on the sabbath, to save life or to destroy it?”
live: Bear with someone (Romans 15:1)
Choose one person whose weakness irritates you, and decide to be patient with that person all this week.
Do good on the Lord's Day (Luke 6:9)
Next Sunday, after the Qurbana, do one work of mercy: visit the sick, an elderly neighbour or a lonely relative.
2027-04-16.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you did not please yourself, but carried the insults meant for us all the way to the Cross, and you rose to give us life. Make us patient with the weak and eager to build up our neighbour. Grant your Church, our parish and our families to live in harmony and to glorify the Father with one voice. When our lives are withered, call us into the middle and say to us, Stretch out your hand, and give us faith to obey. Amen. Alleluia!
altar: The Holy Qurbana is the great work of God on the Lord's Day. At the altar the strong and the weak, those who agree and those who differ, stretch out their hands to receive the one Body of Christ, and are made one voice in praise of the Father.

2027-04-17.title: Third Saturday of Resurrection
2027-04-17.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-04-17.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). Third week of the Resurrection. Saturday, a day on which many keep a loving remembrance of the Blessed Virgin Mary.
2027-04-17.verse: Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I tell you?
theo: James is the most practical writer in the New Testament, and today he asks a question that cannot be dodged: “What good is it, my brothers and sisters, if you say you have faith but do not have works? Can faith save you?” He answers with a scene that everyone can picture. “If a brother or sister is naked and lacks daily food, and one of you says to them, ‘Go in peace; keep warm and eat your fill,’ and yet you do not supply their bodily needs, what is the good of that?” The words in themselves are kind; they are even a blessing. But they cost nothing, and they leave the hungry still hungry. “So faith by itself, if it has no works, is dead.” James is not contradicting Paul, who teaches that we are saved by grace through faith and not by our own achievements. Paul himself speaks of “faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6). The Church has always held the two together: faith is God's unmerited gift, and living faith shows itself in love, as a living tree shows itself in fruit. A faith that never feeds anyone, never forgives anyone, never visits anyone, is like a body without breath. There is a sharp irony in the words “Go in peace”. At the end of every Holy Qurbana the Church sends us out with a blessing of peace. That dismissal is not a polite goodbye; it is a mission. We have received the Body of the Lord who fed the hungry, and we are sent to do the same. The Risen Christ showed his disciples his wounds and then sent them out. Easter faith that stays inside the church walls has not yet understood Easter.

In the Gospel Jesus asks the same question in his own words: “Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I tell you?” To call Jesus Lord is the heart of Christian faith; the first Christians were baptised into that confession. But the title must be matched by obedience, or it becomes empty flattery. Then Jesus tells a story that every builder understands. “I will show you what someone is like who comes to me, hears my words, and acts on them. That one is like a man building a house, who dug deeply and laid the foundation on rock; when a flood arose, the river burst against that house but could not shake it, because it had been well built.” Notice the three verbs: comes, hears, acts. And notice the hard work of digging deep, which no one sees once the house is finished. The other man also heard the words, but he “built a house on the ground without a foundation. When the river burst against it, immediately it fell, and great was the ruin of that house.” Both houses may have looked the same in the dry season. Only the flood showed the difference. Kerala has seen in recent years what floods and landslides can do to houses; the parable is not abstract for us. Every life will meet its flood: sickness, betrayal, failure, the death of someone we love, our own death. The question is what lies under the walls. The rock is Christ himself, the stone the builders rejected, which God raised up at Easter to be the cornerstone (Psalm 118:22). We dig down to that rock by hearing his word and doing it, day after day, in ordinary obedience. On this Saturday the Church looks with love to the Blessed Virgin Mary, the one who heard the word of God and did it most perfectly. When a woman in the crowd blessed the womb that bore Jesus, he answered, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!” (Luke 11:28). Mary is blessed on both counts: she bore the Word in her body because she first received him in faith and obedience. Her “Here am I, the servant of the Lord” is a house built on rock.
outline: Opening
Two houses that look the same until the flood.
Point 1 · Go in peace, keep warm
Kind words without deeds; faith working through love.
Point 2 · Lord, Lord
Calling him Lord and doing what he says.
Point 3 · Dug deeply, built on rock
Christ the cornerstone, and Mary who heard and obeyed.
Take-home line
“Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I tell you?”
live: Supply a bodily need (James 2:16)
Do one concrete act for someone in need this week: a meal, a bag of rice, a fee paid, a hospital visit, instead of only promising to pray.
Dig one level deeper (Luke 6:48)
Pick one teaching of Jesus you already know but do not practise, and begin to put it into practice today.
2027-04-17.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen cornerstone, we call you Lord. Let our lives say it too. Save us from a faith that speaks kind words and leaves the hungry hungry. Give us the patience to dig deep, to hear your word and act on it, so that when the floods come, our house may stand on you. With the Blessed Virgin Mary, who heard the word of God and kept it, let us say each day: be it done to me according to your word. Amen. Alleluia!
altar: The Holy Qurbana ends with a sending in peace. We who have received the Body of the Lord are sent not merely to wish others well but to feed, to clothe and to serve, so that our faith may be alive in works of love.

2027-04-19.title: Fourth Monday of Resurrection
2027-04-19.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The parable of the wicked tenants
2027-04-19.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The fourth week of the Resurrection begins, the day after the Sunday of prayer for vocations. The Gospel stops at verse 16; the saying about the rejected stone follows at once in verse 17.
2027-04-19.verse: Then the owner of the vineyard said, ‘What shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will respect him.’
theo: Paul is near the end of his first letter to Timothy, the young bishop of Ephesus, and he gathers everything into one solemn charge. He does not give it in his own name alone. He calls two witnesses into the room: “In the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession, I charge you to keep the commandment without spot or blame until the manifestation of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The first witness is the God who gives life to all things: in this Easter season we hear that name with new ears, for the God who gives life is the God who raised Jesus from the tomb. The second witness is Jesus standing before Pilate. He was bound, mocked and alone, and yet he spoke the truth calmly: he was a king, and his kingdom was not from this world. That quiet answer is what Paul calls “the good confession”. One verse earlier Paul reminded Timothy that he too had made the good confession “in the presence of many witnesses”, most likely on the day of his Baptism. Every Christian has stood where Timothy stood. At the font we, or our godparents for us, renounced Satan and confessed the faith; at every Holy Qurbana we confess it again in the Creed. Paul's charge is that we keep that confession clean until the Lord appears.

Then the letter breaks into praise, as if Paul cannot mention the coming of Christ without singing. God “will bring about at the right time” the appearing of his Son: “he who is the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords. It is he alone who has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see; to him be honor and eternal dominion. Amen.” These lines sound like a hymn the Church at Ephesus already sang. They tell us two things at once. God is utterly beyond us: no eye can bear his light, no mind can hold him. And yet this same God has made himself known, for the One who stood before Pilate is the image of the invisible God. In the Risen Christ the unapproachable light has come near. On Easter evening the disciples touched him and ate with him. Our Syro-Malabar Qurbana keeps both truths in its prayers: it adores the hidden majesty of God with deep bows and veiled gifts, and in the same celebration it gives us the Body and Blood of the Lord to eat and drink. Holy fear and holy nearness belong together.

In the Gospel Jesus tells a parable in the Temple during his last days in Jerusalem. A man plants a vineyard, leases it to tenants and goes away. At harvest he sends a slave for his share, then a second, then a third; each is beaten and sent away empty-handed. “Then the owner of the vineyard said, ‘What shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will respect him.’” The tenants reason coldly: “This is the heir; let us kill him so that the inheritance may be ours.” They throw him out of the vineyard and kill him. Jesus tells this story a few days before he himself is led outside the city wall to be crucified. The parable is aimed at the leaders who were plotting against him, and Luke says they understood it; it is not a charge against the Jewish people, whom the Church honours as the first tenants of God's vineyard and to whom God's gifts and calling remain irrevocable. The story is a mirror for us. The vineyard is now the Church, and we are its tenants. God still sends his messengers, still asks for the fruit of faith, mercy and justice. The rejected Son is now the Risen Son: the very next line of the Gospel recalls the psalm, “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” Easter is God's answer to the tenants. What men threw out of the vineyard, God set at the corner of a new house, and he has given that house to us. The question for this Monday is simple: when the Owner sends for the fruit, what will he find in my part of the vineyard?
conn: The good confession.

Jesus before Pilate: “For this I was born, and for this I came into the world, to testify to the truth” (John 18:37); Timothy made his own confession “in the presence of many witnesses” (1 Timothy 6:12).
The faithful witness.
Revelation calls Jesus “the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead” (Revelation 1:5): the one who confessed the truth before Pilate is the first to rise.
Unapproachable light.
God is “wrapped in light as with a garment” (Psalm 104:2); yet “the light shines in the darkness” (John 1:5), and the glory of God shines “in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).
The song of the vineyard.
Isaiah sang of God's vineyard that yielded wild grapes (Isaiah 5:1–7); Jesus takes up the same image in this parable.
The beloved son.
At the Jordan the Father says, “You are my Son, the Beloved” (Luke 3:22); in the parable the owner sends “my beloved son”.
The rejected stone.
“The stone that the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone” (Psalm 118:22), quoted by Jesus (Luke 20:17) and by Peter after the Resurrection (Acts 4:11).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana we repeat the good confession in the Creed, and the Son who was thrown out of the vineyard comes to us as the living Bread. The fruit the Father seeks is offered on the altar with the Son's own offering.
The God who dwells in unapproachable light gives himself in the humble form of bread and wine: we approach with reverence and we receive with love.
outline: Opening
A young bishop, a solemn charge, and two witnesses called into the room.
Point 1 · The good confession
Jesus before Pilate, and our confession at the font.
Point 2 · The King of kings in unapproachable light
The hidden God made near in the Risen Christ.
Point 3 · I will send my beloved son
The tenants, the vineyard, and the rejected stone made cornerstone.
Closing image
An old vineyard on a Kerala hillside, still giving fruit because someone tends it each morning.
Take-home line
“I will send my beloved son.”
live: Renew your baptismal promises (1 Timothy 6:12)
Find your Baptism date this week, and on that day say the Creed slowly as your own good confession.
Speak the truth calmly (1 Timothy 6:13)
When you are tempted to lie to escape trouble, remember Jesus before Pilate and say what is true, with gentleness.
Give the Owner his share (Luke 20:10)
Choose one fruit you can give God this week: an hour of prayer, an act of mercy, a gift to the poor.
Bow before the altar
Make a slow, reverent bow when you enter the church: God dwells in light, and he lets us come near.
fathers: St Irenaeus (in substance)

God planted the vineyard of the human race, first in creation and then in choosing a people. He sent the prophets, and at last his own Son. The vineyard was not destroyed but handed on: now it is fenced by the Church and spread throughout the world, and the same God asks from us the fruit he always asked.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

See the patience of the owner. After the first servant was beaten, he sent a second; after the second, a third; after them all, his Son. He did not stop sending because they refused. So God deals with each of us: he does not tire of calling, and we must not tire of answering.
magis: Catechism 2471
Before Pilate, Christ proclaims that he came into the world to bear witness to the truth; the Christian is not to be ashamed of testifying to the Lord.
Catechism 2473
Martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith: it means bearing witness even unto death.
Catechism 755
The Church is a cultivated field, the tillage of God; she is the choice vineyard planted by the heavenly cultivator, and Christ is the true vine.
Catechism 597–598
The responsibility for the trial and death of Jesus cannot be laid on all the Jews of that time or of today; all sinners were the authors of Christ's Passion.
Catechism 1064
The Creed, our profession of faith, is recalled each Sunday: the faith confessed at Baptism is renewed in the liturgy.
saints: This week

19–25 April: fourth week of the Resurrection. Wed 21: in the Latin calendar, St Anselm. Fri 23: in the Latin calendar, St George. Sat 24: in the Syro-Malabar calendar, St George, Martyr (Geevarghese Sahada), an important feast. Sun 25: Fifth Sunday of Resurrection, with Mar Addai; St Mark the Evangelist (25 Apr) gives way to the Sunday this year (verify locally).
2027-04-19.prayer: God our Father, you give life to all things, and you raised your beloved Son whom the builders rejected. Make us faithful tenants of your vineyard, the Church. Keep our baptismal confession clean until the appearing of our Lord, give us courage to speak the truth as he spoke it before Pilate, and let our lives bear the fruit you seek. To you, King of kings and Lord of lords, who dwell in unapproachable light, be honour and eternal dominion, with your Son and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-04-20.title: Fourth Tuesday of Resurrection
2027-04-20.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The life that really is life
For God all things are possible
2027-04-20.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The Gospel follows straight on from the rich young man, who went away grieving because he had many possessions (Matthew 19:16–22).
2027-04-20.verse: But Jesus looked at them and said, “For mortals it is impossible, but for God all things are possible.”
theo: Paul closes his first letter to Timothy with a word for the rich members of the Church at Ephesus. Ephesus was a wealthy port, and the Church there was not made up only of slaves and labourers; there were merchants and householders too. Paul does not tell them that their wealth makes them bad Christians. He tells them where to put their hope: “As for those who in the present age are rich, command them not to be haughty, or to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but rather on God who richly provides us with everything for our enjoyment.” The phrase is beautiful: God is the one who richly provides, and he provides “for our enjoyment”. Creation is a gift, not a trap. The danger lies elsewhere: in pride, and in hoping in what cannot last. So Paul gives the rich a programme: “They are to do good, to be rich in good works, generous, and ready to share, thus storing up for themselves the treasure of a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the life that really is life.” The life that really is life: Paul knows that there is a life that only looks like life, busy and comfortable and empty, and another life that will not end. In this Easter season we know its name. It is the life of the Risen Christ, already planted in us at Baptism.

Then Paul turns to Timothy himself: “Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you.” The word he uses is a banker's word: a deposit, something placed in safe keeping to be returned whole. What has been deposited with Timothy is the faith of the apostles, the Gospel of the crucified and risen Lord. He is not its owner, at liberty to change it; he is its guardian, bound to hand it on intact. Paul warns him against “the profane chatter and contradictions of what is falsely called knowledge”: there were already teachers who claimed a higher, secret knowledge than the plain faith of the Church. The bishops of the Church, successors of Timothy, still have this task, and every parent and catechist shares it. Our forefathers in Kerala called the faith they received from St Thomas the Way of Thomas, Thomma Margam; for centuries they guarded it with little more than the liturgy, the family prayer and the memory of the elders. A deposit is kept not by burying it but by living it and passing it on.

The Gospel picks up just after a rich young man has walked away from Jesus with a sad face. Jesus watches him go and says to his disciples: “Truly I tell you, it will be hard for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven. Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for someone who is rich to enter the kingdom of God.” The picture is deliberately impossible: the largest animal the hearers knew, the smallest opening. The disciples are astounded: “Then who can be saved?” And Jesus looks at them, Matthew notes that look, and says the words that hold the whole Gospel: “For mortals it is impossible, but for God all things are possible.” No one, rich or poor, saves himself. Salvation is God's work, and God can do what we cannot: he can release a heart tied to its possessions, as he can raise a dead man from a sealed tomb. Easter is the proof. Peter, practical as ever, asks what those who have left everything will receive, and Jesus promises a hundredfold, eternal life, and a share in “the renewal of all things”. That renewal began on Easter morning. The last will be first: the Church has always seen this in the poor who are rich in faith, and in those who have given up home and family to follow Christ as priests, religious and missionaries.
conn: Hope not in riches.
“If riches increase, do not set your heart on them” (Psalm 62:10); the rich fool built bigger barns and died that night (Luke 12:16–21).
Rich in good works.
The first believers in Jerusalem “would sell their possessions and goods and distribute the proceeds to all, as any had need” (Acts 2:45).
The deposit of faith.
“Guard the good treasure entrusted to you, with the help of the Holy Spirit living in us” (2 Timothy 1:14).
Nothing too wonderful for God.
“Is anything too wonderful for the LORD?” (Genesis 18:14); the angel to Mary: “nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37).
The rich young man.
He asked what good deed he must do to have eternal life, and went away grieving (Matthew 19:16–22).
The renewal of all things.
“For I am about to create new heavens and a new earth” (Isaiah 65:17); “See, I am making all things new” (Revelation 21:5).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana we bring our offerings to the altar: bread and wine, and the gifts of the people. Whatever we give is first his gift to us, God who richly provides us with everything.
The Body and Blood of the Risen Lord are the pledge of the life that really is life: the hundredfold begins here, at the table where the last are fed first.
outline: Opening
A wealthy port city, and a Church with both slaves and merchants in it.
Point 1 · Not on the uncertainty of riches
God who richly provides, and the life that really is life.
Point 2 · Guard what has been entrusted to you
The deposit of faith, kept by living and handing it on.
Point 3 · For God all things are possible
The camel, the needle and the look of Jesus.
Closing image
A grandmother in Kuttanad who gave away more than she kept, and left her grandchildren a treasure no one could steal.
Take-home line
“For God all things are possible.”
live: Give before you buy (1 Timothy 6:18)
Before your next purchase for yourself this week, set aside something for someone in need.
Name your real treasure (1 Timothy 6:19)
Write down three things you would save in a fire. Ask whether any of them is the life that really is life.
Hand on the faith (1 Timothy 6:20)
Teach a child at home one prayer or one article of the Creed this week.
Ask for the impossible (Matthew 19:26)
Bring to God in prayer one situation you have given up on, and leave it with him.
fathers: St Clement of Alexandria (in substance)

The Lord does not command the rich to throw their goods away, but to banish from the soul the love of money, the passions and the anxieties that choke the seed of life. Wealth is an instrument: used well, it serves justice; used badly, it serves injustice. The one who holds it as God's gift, ready to give, can be saved.
St Basil the Great (in substance)

The bread you keep in your storeroom belongs to the hungry; the coat hanging unused belongs to the one who has none; the shoes rotting in your house belong to the barefoot. You wrong as many people as you could have helped.
magis: Catechism 2544–2547
Jesus calls his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone; poverty of heart frees us from attachment to riches, and the Lord grieves over the rich who find their consolation in abundance.
Catechism 2402–2406
The goods of creation are destined for the whole human race; ownership is a stewardship to be used for the good of others.
Catechism 84
The apostles entrusted the sacred deposit of the faith, contained in Scripture and Tradition, to the whole Church.
Catechism 1817–1821
Hope is the virtue by which we desire eternal life as our happiness, placing our trust in Christ's promises and not in our own strength.
Catechism 1042–1047
At the end of time the universe itself will be renewed; Scripture calls this mysterious renewal the new heavens and the new earth.
saints: This week

19–25 April: fourth week of the Resurrection. Wed 21: in the Latin calendar, St Anselm. Fri 23: in the Latin calendar, St George. Sat 24: in the Syro-Malabar calendar, St George, Martyr (Geevarghese Sahada), an important feast. Sun 25: Fifth Sunday of Resurrection, with Mar Addai; St Mark the Evangelist (25 Apr) gives way to the Sunday this year (verify locally).
2027-04-20.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you looked with love on the rich young man and on your astonished disciples, and you told us that for God all things are possible. Release our hearts from hope in uncertain riches. Make us rich in good works, generous and ready to share, so that we may take hold of the life that really is life. Help our bishops, priests, parents and catechists to guard the faith entrusted to them and to hand it on whole. Renew all things, beginning with us. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-04-21.title: Fourth Wednesday of Resurrection
2027-04-21.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: A priest according to the order of Melchizedek
2027-04-21.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). In the Latin calendar today is the memorial of St Anselm, bishop and doctor of the Church.
2027-04-21.verse: Without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but resembling the Son of God, he remains a priest forever.
theo: The Letter to the Hebrews reaches back to one of the most mysterious figures of the Old Testament. In Genesis 14 Abram returns from rescuing his nephew Lot, and a stranger comes out to meet him: “And King Melchizedek of Salem brought out bread and wine; he was priest of God Most High.” He blesses Abram, and Abram gives him a tenth of everything. Then Melchizedek vanishes from the story. Centuries later Psalm 110 speaks of a king whom God has sworn to make “a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” Hebrews brings these two passages together and sees in them a portrait of Christ. Melchizedek's name means “king of righteousness”; he is king of Salem, that is, “king of peace”. Scripture gives him no father or mother, no genealogy, no birth or death: “resembling the Son of God, he remains a priest forever.” The writer does not say Melchizedek was an angel or a ghost. He says that Scripture's silence about his origin and end makes him a living picture of the true Priest, who has no beginning as the eternal Son and no end as the Risen One.

Then the letter argues, in the careful way of a rabbi, that this priesthood is greater than the priesthood of Levi. Abraham, the father of the whole people and the one who “had received the promises”, received a blessing from Melchizedek and gave him tithes: “It is beyond dispute that the inferior is blessed by the superior.” Levi, still unborn, was in a sense in Abraham and paid tithes through him. Then comes a line that rings with Easter: “In the one case, tithes are received by those who are mortal; in the other, by one of whom it is testified that he lives.” The Levitical priests died one after another, and their office passed from father to son. Christ's priesthood does not pass to anyone, for, as the same chapter says a little later, “he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever. Consequently he is able for all time to save those who approach God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them.” The Resurrection is not only the end of Christ's suffering; it is the beginning of his eternal priesthood. At this moment the Risen Lord stands before the Father, interceding for us. The Fathers of the Church loved to point out that Melchizedek brought out bread and wine. In every Holy Qurbana the eternal Priest offers himself under those same signs; our priests stand at the altar not in their own name but in his.

In the Gospel Jesus answers those who challenged him for healing on the sabbath. He speaks of witnesses, as in a court of law: the Law required two or three witnesses before a charge could stand. “If I testify about myself, my testimony is not true.” So he calls his witnesses. First John the Baptist: “He was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light.” Then a greater witness: “The works that the Father has given me to complete, the very works that I am doing, testify on my behalf that the Father has sent me.” And behind the works, the Father himself: “And the Father who sent me has himself testified on my behalf.” Jesus is not seeking his own glory: “I seek to do not my own will but the will of him who sent me.” The Church reads this passage in Easter time because the Resurrection is the Father's great testimony to his Son. When the Father raised Jesus from the dead, he declared before the whole world that this was his Son. The apostles then became witnesses in their turn, and so must we. The world will not believe because we argue well; it believes when it sees the works that the Risen Lord still does through his Church.
conn: Bread and wine.
“And King Melchizedek of Salem brought out bread and wine; he was priest of God Most High” (Genesis 14:18).
A priest forever.
“The LORD has sworn and will not change his mind, ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek’” (Psalm 110:4), quoted in Hebrews 5:6 and 7:17.
He always lives to intercede.

Christ “holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever” (Hebrews 7:24–25); “It is Christ Jesus, who died, yes, who was raised, who is at the right hand of God, who indeed intercedes for us” (Romans 8:34).
Two or three witnesses.
“Only on the evidence of two or three witnesses shall a charge be sustained” (Deuteronomy 19:15); Jesus says the same in John 8:17–18.
The burning lamp.
John the Baptist “came as a witness to testify to the light” (John 1:7); he said, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).
The Father's testimony.
At the Jordan a voice from heaven said, “This is my Son, the Beloved” (Matthew 3:17); in the Resurrection the Father declared Jesus Son of God with power (Romans 1:4).
altar: The Qurbana is the offering of the Priest according to the order of Melchizedek: bread and wine brought to the altar become, by the power of the Holy Spirit, the Body and Blood of the Risen Lord, who lives forever to intercede for us.
Our priests act in the person of Christ; there is one Priest and one Sacrifice, made present on every altar of the world.
outline: Opening
A stranger with bread and wine on the road of Abram's return.
Point 1 · King of righteousness, king of peace
Melchizedek as a living picture of Christ.
Point 2 · One of whom it is testified that he lives
The Risen Priest who always intercedes.
Point 3 · The witnesses
John the lamp, the works, and the Father's testimony.
Closing image
A priest raising the bread and the cup at a village altar, and behind him the eternal Priest.
Take-home line
“He always lives to make intercession for them.”
live: Pray for priests (Hebrews 7:3)
Pray today by name for the priest who baptised you and for your parish priest.
Lean on Christ's intercession (Hebrews 7:25)
When you cannot find words in prayer, say: Lord Jesus, you always live to intercede for me; pray for me now.
Give your tithe of time (Hebrews 7:2)
Give God the first part of the day: begin it with prayer before your phone.
Be a lamp (John 5:35)
Let one good work this week point beyond yourself to Christ, as John the Baptist did.
fathers: St Cyprian of Carthage (in substance)

In the priest Melchizedek we see the mystery of the Lord's sacrifice prefigured: he offered bread and wine and blessed Abraham. Who is more a priest of the Most High than our Lord Jesus Christ, who offered to God the Father the very same thing Melchizedek had offered, bread and wine, that is, his Body and Blood?
St Ambrose (in substance)

Who is the king of righteousness, the king of peace, without beginning of days or end of life, if not Christ? Melchizedek received Abraham with bread and wine; so the sacraments of the Church are older than the synagogue, and the figure came before the law.
magis: Catechism 1333
The Church sees in the gesture of the king-priest Melchizedek, who brought out bread and wine, a prefiguring of her own offering.
Catechism 1544–1545

Everything that the priesthood of the Old Covenant prefigured finds its fulfilment in Christ, the one high priest after the order of Melchizedek; the ministerial priesthood shares in his one priesthood.
Catechism 662
Christ, the high priest of the good things to come, always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him.
Catechism 548
The signs worked by Jesus attest that the Father has sent him; they invite belief in him.
Catechism 523
St John the Baptist is the Lord's immediate precursor, sent to prepare his way; he is more than a prophet.
saints: Today
Latin calendar: St Anselm (1033–1109), born at Aosta, monk and abbot of Bec in Normandy, Archbishop of Canterbury, doctor of the Church, who described theology as faith seeking understanding.

19–25 April: fourth week of the Resurrection. Wed 21: in the Latin calendar, St Anselm. Fri 23: in the Latin calendar, St George. Sat 24: in the Syro-Malabar calendar, St George, Martyr (Geevarghese Sahada), an important feast. Sun 25: Fifth Sunday of Resurrection, with Mar Addai; St Mark the Evangelist (25 Apr) gives way to the Sunday this year (verify locally).
2027-04-21.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, eternal Priest according to the order of Melchizedek, King of righteousness and King of peace, you live for ever to make intercession for us. Accept the bread and wine we bring, and make them your Body and Blood. Bless our priests, who stand at the altar in your name. Make us witnesses like John, burning and shining lamps, so that the world may see in our works that the Father has sent you. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-04-22.title: Fourth Thursday of Resurrection
2027-04-22.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Honour with the lips, and the heart far away
2027-04-22.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). A day to examine the heart: the readings speak of teachers who deny the Lord who bought them, and of worship that stays on the lips.
2027-04-22.verse: This people honors me with their lips, but their hearts are far from me;
theo: The Second Letter of Peter was written for Christians who had received the faith from the apostles and were now hearing other voices. Peter does not pretend the Church will be spared trouble from within: “But false prophets also arose among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive opinions. They will even deny the Master who bought them—bringing swift destruction on themselves.” Two things mark these false teachers. They work secretly, slipping their opinions in beside the true faith so that the change is hardly noticed. And they deny the Master who bought them. The word is the language of the slave market: Christ has paid the price for us, with his own Blood, and we belong to him. A teaching that empties the Cross, or reduces the Resurrection to a pleasant idea, or makes Jesus one teacher among many, denies the very Lord who bought us. Peter adds a sad note: “many will follow their licentious ways, and because of these teachers the way of truth will be maligned.” False doctrine and loose living travel together, and when Christians live badly, the world speaks ill of the faith itself. Finally, “in their greed they will exploit you with deceptive words.” Then as now, some made religion a business.

How do we recognise a false teacher? The Church has never answered by asking each Christian to judge alone. The same letter reminds its readers to remember “the commandment of the Lord and Savior spoken through your apostles” (2 Peter 3:2). The test is the faith of the apostles, handed down in the Scriptures, kept in the living Tradition and taught by the bishops in communion with the successor of Peter. Our own Church carries this memory deeply. For centuries the Thomas Christians of Kerala lived the faith received from the apostle with very few books; when strangers came with new teachings, the people asked one question: is this what our fathers received? The Easter season is a good time to hold fast to the apostolic faith, because it rests on the apostles' witness to the Risen Lord. They did not hand on an opinion. They handed on what they had seen and heard and touched. A sound test for any new voice, on a screen or in a meeting, is this: does it lead me to Christ crucified and risen, to the sacraments and to love of the Church, or away from them?

In the Gospel some Pharisees and scribes come from Jerusalem and ask why the disciples do not wash their hands before eating, as the tradition of the elders required. The washing was a religious rite, not a matter of hygiene, and many devout people kept it with love. Jesus does not attack washing; he exposes a misuse. Some had found a way to declare their savings dedicated to God, Korban, so that they need not support their aged parents: “So, for the sake of your tradition, you make void the word of God.” And he quotes Isaiah: “This people honors me with their lips, but their hearts are far from me; in vain do they worship me, teaching human precepts as doctrines.” This is a word for religious people of every age, and first for us. Jesus is not speaking against the Jewish people, nor against tradition as such; he himself kept the feasts and prayed in the synagogue, and the Church lives by the apostolic Tradition. He is speaking against any custom, ours included, that becomes a way to avoid love. A Syro-Malabar Christian may keep every fast, every feast and every family custom, and still neglect an old father or speak bitterly of a neighbour. Then our worship is lip-service. Easter asks for a new heart: the Risen Lord does not want only our lips at the Qurbana, but hearts that go home and honour father and mother.
conn: False prophets.
“Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you; they are deluding you” (Jeremiah 23:16); Jesus warns, “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing” (Matthew 7:15).
Bought with a price.
“For you were bought with a price; therefore glorify God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:20); “you were ransomed… with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19).
Hold fast to the traditions.
“Stand firm and hold fast to the traditions that you were taught by us, either by word of mouth or by our letter” (2 Thessalonians 2:15).
Honour father and mother.
The fourth commandment (Exodus 20:12), “the first commandment with a promise” (Ephesians 6:2).
Lips and heart.
Jesus quotes Isaiah 29:13; Paul writes, “one believes with the heart and so is justified, and one confesses with the mouth and so is saved” (Romans 10:10).
A new heart.
“A new heart I will give you, and a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezekiel 36:26).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Church prays the words handed down from the apostles: this is the Tradition that leads us to the Lord who bought us with his Blood, present on the altar.
Before we come to Communion we are invited to make peace and to purify the heart; the Lord wants lips that confess him and hearts that are near him.
outline: Opening
A young Church hearing new voices.
Point 1 · They will deny the Master who bought them
False teachers then and now.
Point 2 · Hold fast to the apostolic faith
The test of what our fathers received.
Point 3 · Lips near, hearts far
Customs that serve love, and customs that avoid it.
Closing image
A son who stops making excuses and goes to sit with his old father on the veranda.
Take-home line
“This people honors me with their lips, but their hearts are far from me.”
live: Test the voices (2 Peter 2:1)
Before you share a religious video or message, ask: does it lead to Christ, the sacraments and the Church?
Remember the price (1 Corinthians 6:20)
Look at a crucifix today and say: Lord, you bought me; I am yours.
Honour your parents (Matthew 15:4)
Do one concrete thing this week for your parents or an elderly relative: a visit, a call, a task done.
Pray with the heart (Matthew 15:8)
At the Qurbana this week, choose one prayer and mean every word of it.
fathers: St Irenaeus (in substance)

The tradition of the apostles, made known throughout the whole world, can be found in every Church by those who wish to see the truth. We can name those whom the apostles appointed bishops and their successors down to our own time; they taught nothing like the fantasies of the heretics. The truth is easy to find, for the apostles deposited it in the Church as in a rich treasury.
St Augustine (in substance)

Sing to God not only with the voice but with the heart. Many have the voice and are silent within; others are silent and their heart cries to God. Let your life sing: when the voice is quiet, let your love be heard.
magis: Catechism 77–83

The apostles entrusted the Gospel to their successors, the bishops; Sacred Tradition and Sacred Scripture are bound together, flowing from the same divine wellspring; ecclesial traditions are distinct from the apostolic Tradition and can be retained, modified or abandoned.
Catechism 85–88
The task of authentically interpreting the word of God has been entrusted to the living teaching office of the Church, which serves the word of God and is not above it.
Catechism 2214–2220
The fourth commandment: grown children have duties toward their parents; they must give them material and moral support in old age and in sickness.
Catechism 2100
Outward sacrifice, to be genuine, must be the expression of spiritual sacrifice: a broken and contrite heart.
Catechism 595–597
The Jews are not collectively responsible for the death of Jesus; Jesus' disputes with some Pharisees do not justify blame on the Jewish people.
saints: This week

19–25 April: fourth week of the Resurrection. Wed 21: in the Latin calendar, St Anselm. Fri 23: in the Latin calendar, St George. Sat 24: in the Syro-Malabar calendar, St George, Martyr (Geevarghese Sahada), an important feast. Sun 25: Fifth Sunday of Resurrection, with Mar Addai; St Mark the Evangelist (25 Apr) gives way to the Sunday this year (verify locally).
2027-04-22.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you bought us with your precious Blood, and you want our hearts, not only our lips. Keep us faithful to the faith of the apostles, handed down in your Church, and guard us from voices that would lead us away from you. Deliver us from customs that excuse us from love. Give us new hearts that honour our parents, care for the elderly and worship you in spirit and truth. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-04-23.title: Fourth Friday of Resurrection
2027-04-23.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-04-23.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). In the Latin calendar today is St George, martyr; the Syro-Malabar calendar keeps the feast of St George (Geevarghese Sahada) tomorrow, 24 April (verify locally). Even in the Easter season every Friday recalls the Lord's Passion; follow your eparchy's norms on Friday penance.
2027-04-23.verse: Therefore it says, “Sleeper, awake! Rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.”
theo: In the middle of a page of practical advice, Paul suddenly quotes a few lines that sound like a song: “Sleeper, awake! Rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.” Many scholars think this was a hymn sung at Baptism in the first Christian communities. One can imagine the newly baptised coming up from the water while the community sang it over them. The words gather the whole of Easter into three short lines: we were asleep, we were dead, and Christ, the Sun risen from the tomb, has shone on us. Paul has just said that “everything exposed by the light becomes visible”. The light of Christ does not only warm us; it shows us the truth about ourselves, and what is brought into his light is healed. That is why the Church has always loved to call Baptism illumination. In the Easter season the paschal candle stands near the altar in some of our churches, and the newly baptised receive a lit candle: they are sleepers who have been woken and dead who have risen.

Then Paul draws the consequences for daily life. “Be careful then how you live, not as unwise people but as wise, making the most of the time, because the days are evil.” The Christian is awake, and an awake person does not waste the day. He warns against drunkenness, which dulls the mind and wrecks families, and offers another kind of fullness instead: “be filled with the Spirit, as you sing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs among yourselves, singing and making melody to the Lord in your hearts, giving thanks to God the Father at all times and for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The Spirit-filled Church is a singing and thankful Church. Our Syro-Malabar tradition knows this well: the Qurbana is sung, the hours of prayer are sung, and the homes of our grandparents rang each evening with the family prayer and its songs. Paul ends with a word that opens the next section on family life: “Be subject to one another out of reverence for Christ.” Mutual service is the fruit of the Spirit; a home where each gives way to the other for Christ's sake is already full of his light.

The Gospel is Mark's account of the feeding of the five thousand. It is late, the place is deserted, and the disciples want to send the crowd away to buy food. Jesus answers: “You give them something to eat.” They protest that two hundred denarii would hardly be enough. “How many loaves have you? Go and see.” Five, and two fish. Then Mark describes what Jesus does with words every Christian recognises: “Taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven, and blessed and broke the loaves, and gave them to his disciples to set before the people.” Took, blessed, broke, gave: these are the very actions of the Last Supper and of every Qurbana. All ate and were filled, and twelve baskets of fragments were left over, one for each apostle, as if to say that the Church will never run out of this bread. Two lessons stand out for this Easter Friday. First, Jesus works through the disciples: he does not drop bread from the sky but asks them to bring what little they have and to hand it out. Second, he feeds the people with abundance: the Risen Lord still gives himself in the Eucharist to all who come, and he still says to his Church in the face of every hunger, of body and of soul, “You give them something to eat.”
conn: Arise, shine.
“Arise, shine; for your light has come, and the glory of the LORD has risen upon you” (Isaiah 60:1).
Children of light.
“For once you were darkness, but now in the Lord you are light. Live as children of light” (Ephesians 5:8).
Sing to the Lord.
“O sing to the LORD a new song; sing to the LORD, all the earth” (Psalm 96:1); “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly… sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs to God” (Colossians 3:16).
Elisha's loaves.
“They shall eat and have some left” (2 Kings 4:43–44): twenty barley loaves for a hundred people.
The boy with the loaves.
John's account adds that the five barley loaves and two fish belonged to a boy (John 6:9).
Took, blessed, broke, gave.
The same four actions at the Last Supper (Mark 14:22) and at Emmaus, where the disciples knew him “in the breaking of the bread” (Luke 24:30–35).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Lord does again what he did in the deserted place: he takes the bread, gives thanks, breaks it and gives it through his ministers, and the bread is now his own Body, the true Bread from heaven.
Our small offerings brought to the altar are like the five loaves: little in our hands, abundant in his.
outline: Opening
A baptismal hymn: sleeper, awake!
Point 1 · Christ will shine on you
Baptism as illumination, and the light that heals.
Point 2 · Be filled with the Spirit
Wise living, singing and thanksgiving at all times.
Point 3 · You give them something to eat
Five loaves, four actions and twelve baskets.
Closing image
A parish kitchen on a Friday evening where a few volunteers feed many.
Take-home line
“Sleeper, awake! Rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.”
live: Wake up to the day (Ephesians 5:16)
Begin tomorrow with a short prayer of light: Christ, shine on me today.
Sing at home (Ephesians 5:19)
Sing one hymn together as a family at evening prayer this week.
Give thanks for everything (Ephesians 5:20)
Before sleep tonight, name three things you are thankful for, including one that was hard.
Bring your loaves (Mark 6:38)
Offer one small skill or a little money to a parish or charity that feeds the hungry.
fathers: St Clement of Alexandria (in substance)

The Lord says, Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ the Lord will shine on you: the Sun of the Resurrection, begotten before the morning star, who gives life by his own rays. Let us open our eyes to that light and walk in the day.
St Ephrem the Syrian (in substance)
In your Bread is hidden the Spirit who cannot be consumed; in your Wine dwells the Fire that cannot be drunk. The Spirit in your Bread, the Fire in your Wine: a wonder that our lips receive.
magis: Catechism 1216
Baptism is called enlightenment, because those who receive it are enlightened in their understanding; having received the Word, the true light, the baptised person becomes a son of light.
Catechism 1335

The miracles of the multiplication of the loaves, when the Lord said the blessing, broke and distributed the loaves through his disciples to feed the multitude, prefigure the superabundance of this unique bread of his Eucharist.
Catechism 2637–2638
Thanksgiving characterises the prayer of the Church; every event and need can become an offering of thanksgiving.
Catechism 1156–1158
Song and music are closely linked to the liturgy; singing with the heart is a sign of the Church's prayer.
Catechism 2443–2449
God blesses those who come to the aid of the poor; love for the poor is part of the Church's constant tradition.

Sat 24: in the Syro-Malabar calendar, St George, Martyr (Geevarghese Sahada), an important feast. Sun 25: Fifth Sunday of Resurrection, with Mar Addai; St Mark the Evangelist (25 Apr) gives way to the Sunday this year (verify locally).
2027-04-23.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Sun of the Resurrection, you woke us from sleep and raised us from death in Baptism; shine on us today. Fill us with your Holy Spirit, so that we may live wisely, sing your praises and give thanks to the Father at all times and for everything. As you fed the hungry crowd in the deserted place, feed us with the Bread of your Body, and make us generous to all who hunger. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-04-24.title: Fourth Saturday of Resurrection · St George, Martyr (Geevarghese Sahada)
2027-04-24.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Daniel in the den of lions
James is killed; the Church prays for Peter
Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it
2027-04-24.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). St George, Martyr, is listed in the First Set calendar as an important feast, with the readings above; the calendar gives longer forms: Acts 12:1–23; 2 Corinthians 12:1–14; Matthew 10:37–42 with 16:24–27 and 19:29–30. Weekday readings of the Fourth Saturday: 1 Corinthians 14:20–25; Mark 6:1–6. In the Latin calendar St George was kept yesterday, 23 April. Follow your eparchy and parish on which readings are used (verify locally).
2027-04-24.verse: My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.
theo: Few saints are loved across so many Churches and nations as St George. In the Syriac tradition he is Mar Geevarghese Sahada, George the Martyr; Sahada means witness, the one who bears testimony with his blood. Kerala is full of his churches and his name: in Christian families of every tradition, boys are called Geevarghese, Varghese, Varkey and George, and great pilgrim churches such as Aruvithura and Edathua draw crowds who come to him with their fears and their vows. What do we know of him? The early Church honoured his tomb at Lydda, the town in Palestine where Peter once healed Aeneas, and pilgrims were visiting it by the sixth century. The tradition remembers him as a soldier in the Roman army who refused to deny Christ in the great persecution under the emperor Diocletian, at the beginning of the fourth century, and who was tortured and beheaded. An ancient list of writings, attributed to Pope Gelasius at the end of the fifth century but probably compiled somewhat later, named him among those saints whose names are rightly honoured but whose deeds are known only to God. The famous story of the dragon came much later, in the Middle Ages, and is a legend, not history; the Church reads it as a picture of the truth, that the martyr's faith overcomes the ancient serpent. The history is short, but it is enough: a man under orders, with everything to lose, who chose Christ above his career and his life.

The readings chosen for the feast gather around that choice. Daniel, a Jewish exile serving the king of the Medes and Persians, keeps praying to his God three times a day although a royal decree has made it a crime. His enemies report him, and the king, who loves Daniel, cannot revoke his own law. Daniel is thrown to the lions and a stone is sealed over the mouth of the den. At dawn the king runs to the den and calls out: “O Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God whom you faithfully serve been able to deliver you from the lions?” And Daniel answers: “My God sent his angel and shut the lions’ mouths so that they would not hurt me.” He comes up unharmed, “because he had trusted in his God.” The scene speaks of Easter: a stone sealed, a long night, a hurried dawn visit, and the servant of God alive. The reading ends grimly with the punishment of the accusers, as the law of that ancient kingdom demanded; Christ has taught us instead to pray for those who persecute us, and the martyrs, St George among them, died forgiving.

The Acts of the Apostles takes us to the first martyrdom among the twelve. “About that time King Herod laid violent hands upon some who belonged to the church. He had James, the brother of John, killed with the sword.” Seeing that this won him favour with some, he arrested Peter too, during the days of Unleavened Bread, intending to bring him out after the Passover. Herod, Agrippa I, was a ruler anxious to please, and Luke shows a politician's calculation; the Church does not read this as blame on the Jewish people, from whom the apostles themselves came. Then comes the verse that has carried the Church through every persecution: “While Peter was kept in prison, the church prayed fervently to God for him.” James gave his life; Peter was released by an angel; both were held in the Church's prayer. In his letter to the Corinthians Paul reveals the secret of such courage. He had been caught up in visions, yet God left him “a thorn… in the flesh” and would not remove it. Three times he begged the Lord, and the answer came: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.” So Paul concludes: “whenever I am weak, then I am strong.” Martyrs are not people without fear. They are weak people who have let the power of the Risen Christ dwell in them.

The Gospel states the cost plainly: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me… and whoever does not take up the cross and follow me is not worthy of me.” These are hard words in a culture like ours, where family is everything. Jesus does not ask us to love our families less; he asks to be loved first, so that our love for them may be pure and strong. Then he gives the law of Easter: “Those who find their life will lose it, and those who lose their life for my sake will find it.” George lost his rank, his safety and his life, and found them all again in the Risen Lord; seventeen centuries later we still keep his day. Most of us will not be asked to die for Christ. But we are asked every day to lose a little life for him: to refuse a dishonest deal, to keep Sunday holy when work demands it, to stand by the faith in an office or a college where it is mocked. The Gospel ends with a tender promise: even “a cup of cold water” given to one of Christ's little ones will not lose its reward. On this feast we pray for Cardinal Mar George Alencherry, Major Archbishop emeritus, for all bishops, priests and faithful who bear the name of St George, and for Christians who are persecuted today, that they may be strong in weakness, as he was.
conn: They shut the mouths of lions.
The heroes of faith “through faith conquered kingdoms, administered justice, obtained promises, shut the mouths of lions” (Hebrews 11:33).
The angel of the Lord.
“The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them” (Psalm 34:7); an angel later frees Peter from prison (Acts 12:6–11).
The cup James drank.
Jesus had asked James and John, “Are you able to drink the cup that I drink?” and told them, “The cup that I drink you will drink” (Mark 10:38–39).
Strength to the weak.
“He gives power to the faint, and strengthens the powerless” (Isaiah 40:29).
Lose life to find it.
“If any want to become my followers, let them deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me” (Matthew 16:24), one of the longer forms given for today.
The crown of life.
“Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Revelation 2:10); “the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God” (Wisdom 3:1).
altar: The martyrs have always been honoured at the altar: their witness flows from the Sacrifice of Christ, whom they followed to the end. At the Holy Qurbana we offer the same Sacrifice and ask to share their courage.
The Body and Blood of the Risen Lord are the strength of the weak: in Communion his power comes to dwell in us, as Paul says, so that we too may stand firm.
outline: Opening
A soldier with everything to lose, and the name Geevarghese in Kerala homes.
Point 1 · The God who shut the lions' mouths
Daniel's faithful prayer and the sealed stone.
Point 2 · The Church prayed fervently
James killed, Peter imprisoned, the community on its knees.
Point 3 · Power made perfect in weakness
Paul's thorn and the secret of the martyrs.
Point 4 · Lose your life to find it
Christ loved first, and the cup of cold water.
Closing image
A small boy named Geevarghese lighting a candle before the saint's image, and his grandmother teaching him whose name he bears.
Take-home line
“My grace is sufficient for you.”
live: Pray like Daniel (Daniel 6:13)
Keep three short moments of prayer today, morning, noon and night, whatever else happens.
Pray for the persecuted (Acts 12:5)
Pray a decade of the rosary for Christians in prison or danger for their faith.
Offer your weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9)
Name one weakness you are ashamed of and give it to Christ: Lord, let your power dwell here.
Give a cup of water (Matthew 10:42)
Do one small, hidden kindness today for someone who cannot repay you.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

It is not the punishment but the cause that makes the martyr. Many suffer; the martyr suffers for Christ and for the truth. Let us not admire only their blood, but the faith for which it was shed, and imitate that faith in our own trials.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Paul did not say, My grace takes away your weakness, but, My grace is sufficient for you. The thorn remained, so that the power might be seen to be God's. When we are weak and still stand, everyone sees that it is grace that holds us up.
magis: Catechism 2473–2474
Martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith; the Church has painstakingly collected the records of those who persevered to the end in witnessing to their faith.
Catechism 1173
When the Church keeps the memorials of martyrs and other saints during the annual cycle, she proclaims the Paschal mystery in those who have suffered and have been glorified with Christ.
Catechism 273
Only faith can embrace the mysterious ways of God's almighty power; this faith glories in its weaknesses in order to draw to itself Christ's power.
Catechism 956
The saints in heaven do not cease to intercede for us with the Father; their fraternal concern is the greatest help to our weakness.
Respect for parents and family is a duty; yet the first vocation of the Christian is to follow Jesus, and family ties, though important, are not absolute.
saints: Today

St George, Martyr (Geevarghese Sahada): in the First Set calendar an important feast; patron of many churches and families in Kerala, including the pilgrim churches of Aruvithura and Edathua. Pray for Cardinal Mar George Alencherry, Major Archbishop emeritus, and for all who bear the name George.
This week

19–25 April: fourth week of the Resurrection. Wed 21: in the Latin calendar, St Anselm. Fri 23: in the Latin calendar, St George. Sat 24: in the Syro-Malabar calendar, St George, Martyr (Geevarghese Sahada), an important feast. Sun 25: Fifth Sunday of Resurrection, with Mar Addai; St Mark the Evangelist (25 Apr) gives way to the Sunday this year (verify locally).
2027-04-24.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you gave St George the courage to choose you above his rank, his safety and his life. By his prayers, strengthen all who suffer for your name. As you shut the lions' mouths for Daniel and answered the prayer of the Church for Peter, protect your Church today. Let your power be made perfect in our weakness, so that we may love you first, take up our cross and find our life in you. Bless Cardinal Mar George Alencherry and all who bear the name of St George. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-04-26.title: Fifth Monday of Resurrection
2027-04-26.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Do not be surprised at the fiery ordeal
2027-04-26.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost.
2027-04-26.verse: For just as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh, so the Son of Man will be to this generation.
theo: The crowds around Jesus keep growing, and with the crowds grows the demand for proof. They want a sign from heaven, something so overwhelming that no one could doubt. Jesus refuses: “This generation is an evil generation; it asks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah.” Then he explains: “For just as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh, so the Son of Man will be to this generation.” What was the sign of Jonah? A prophet who went down into the depths, swallowed up as if dead, and came back after three days to preach. Matthew spells it out: “For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the sea monster, so for three days and three nights the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12:40). We read this Gospel four weeks after Easter, and so we hear it as the disciples heard it after the Resurrection: the sign has been given. The tomb is empty. There will be no other sign greater than this one, and no sign is needed beyond it. The Church still meets people who ask for a proof that would force them to believe. She can only point, as Jesus did, to the Crucified One who rose on the third day, and to the lives of those who have met him.

Jesus then names two foreigners who will rise at the judgment and put his hearers to shame. The queen of the South travelled from the ends of the earth just to listen to Solomon's wisdom; the people of Nineveh, a pagan city, “repented at the proclamation of Jonah”. And the refrain comes twice: “see, something greater than Solomon is here!”, “see, something greater than Jonah is here!” Jesus does not speak against his own people; he speaks as a prophet of Israel, calling his generation to listen as Nineveh listened. Every generation, ours included, is in the same place. Our Syro-Malabar Church keeps the memory of Nineveh alive every year in the Moonnu Nombu, the three days' fast of the Ninevites before the Great Fast, when the faithful flock to Kuravilangad and to many other churches and fast with the hope of the people who believed a preacher of repentance. Today, in the bright weeks of Easter, the same story speaks of joy rather than sackcloth: if Nineveh changed at the voice of Jonah, how much more should we change at the voice of the One who came back from the dead, greater than Jonah and greater than Solomon.

Peter writes to Christians who are discovering that the Risen Lord does not take them out of trouble. “Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery ordeal that is taking place among you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you.” Suffering for Christ is not a sign that something has gone wrong; it is part of belonging to him. “But rejoice insofar as you are sharing Christ's sufferings, so that you may also be glad and shout for joy when his glory is revealed.” The joy of Easter is not cancelled by the Cross; it shines through it. Peter is precise: there is no glory in suffering for doing wrong, but “if any of you suffers as a Christian, do not consider it a disgrace, but glorify God because you bear this name.” The name Christian, first given at Antioch (Acts 11:26), was perhaps meant as mockery; the martyrs wore it as a crown. The fiery ordeal comes in many sizes: the student laughed at for making the sign of the Cross before a meal, the employee passed over for refusing to falsify an account, the believers in many lands who lose homes and lives for the faith. To all of them Peter gives one instruction: “let those suffering in accordance with God's will entrust themselves to a faithful Creator, while continuing to do good.” Entrust, and keep doing good. That is how the sign of Jonah is lived in an ordinary Christian life: going down into trouble without losing faith, and coming up again with the light of the Resurrection.
outline: Opening
Ask: what sign am I still waiting for before I give myself fully to Christ?
Point 1 · No sign but the sign of Jonah
Three days in the depths, and the empty tomb.
Point 2 · Something greater is here
Nineveh repented, the queen came from afar; what about us?
Point 3 · Do not be surprised at the fiery ordeal
Suffering as a Christian, and entrusting ourselves to a faithful Creator.
Take-home line
“See, something greater than Jonah is here!”
live: Stop asking for more signs (Luke 11:29)
Make an act of faith today in the Risen Lord, without conditions: Lord, you are risen; that is enough for me.
Bear the name with joy (1 Peter 4:16)
Make the sign of the Cross openly before one meal today, wherever you are, and pray for Christians who suffer for the name.
fathers: St Cyril of Jerusalem (in substance)

Jonah was cast into the belly of the great fish, but Christ went down of his own will into the heart of the earth. Jonah was brought up again to preach repentance to Nineveh; Christ rose to call the whole world to repentance and life. If the story of Jonah is believed, how much more the Resurrection of the Lord.
St Ignatius of Antioch (in substance)

On his way to martyrdom he begged the Christians of Rome not to prevent his death: let me be food for the beasts, through whom I may reach God. I am the wheat of God, ground by their teeth, that I may be found the pure bread of Christ.
magis: Catechism 994
Jesus links faith in the resurrection to his own person and gives the sign of Jonah, the sign of the temple, as the sign of his own Resurrection.
Catechism 1430–1431
Interior repentance is a radical reorientation of our whole life, a return to God with all our heart, as Nineveh turned at the preaching of Jonah.
Catechism 2473
Martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith; the martyr bears witness to Christ who died and rose, to whom he is united by charity.
2027-04-26.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you went down into the heart of the earth and rose on the third day: you are the sign of Jonah given to every generation. Forgive us for asking for more proof when you have already given us yourself. Give us the humility of Nineveh to repent at your word, and the courage of your martyrs to bear your name without shame. When the fiery ordeal comes, teach us to entrust ourselves to the faithful Creator and to go on doing good, until your glory is revealed and we shout for joy. Amen. Alleluia!
altar: The Holy Qurbana is the sign of Jonah placed in our hands: the Lord who went down into death and rose again gives us his Body and Blood. Something greater than Solomon and greater than Jonah is here on the altar.

2027-04-27.title: Fifth Tuesday of Resurrection
2027-04-27.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Live according to the word of God
Bear fruit by the grace given
2027-04-27.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost.
2027-04-27.verse: But be doers of the word, and not merely hearers who deceive themselves.
theo: James writes like a man who has watched many people come out of church unchanged. “But be doers of the word, and not merely hearers who deceive themselves.” Then he gives an image everyone understands: “For if any are hearers of the word and not doers, they are like those who look at themselves in a mirror; for they look at themselves and, on going away, immediately forget what they were like.” In Aranmula, on the banks of the Pampa, craftsmen still make the famous metal mirror, the Aranmula kannadi, polished for days until it shows a face without distortion. Nobody buys such a mirror only to forget their face. The word of God is a mirror like that: it shows us exactly who we are, both our sins and our dignity as children of God. The danger James sees is not that we refuse to look, but that we look, nod, and walk away. In this Easter season the Risen Lord has spoken to us Sunday after Sunday. The question is whether anything has changed between one Sunday and the next.

James then turns to the true test of religion. First the tongue: “If any think they are religious, and do not bridle their tongues but deceive their hearts, their religion is worthless.” A Christian who prays the long prayers of the Qurbana and then tears a neighbour to pieces on the way home has not yet understood what he prayed. Then the hands: “Religion that is pure and undefiled before God, the Father, is this: to care for orphans and widows in their distress, and to keep oneself unstained by the world.” Two things, held together: mercy towards the weakest, and purity of life. Kerala's Christians have a long history of the first. Religious sisters and brothers, priests and lay people have built homes for children without parents, for the abandoned elderly, for the sick whom no one wanted, and many of these houses are still kept going by the small gifts of ordinary parishes. James calls this not a hobby for the generous but the heart of religion. Every Easter Christian is invited to ask: whom do I visit? Which orphan, which widow, which lonely old man knows me by name?

In the Gospel Jesus walks into Jerusalem in the morning, hungry. He sees a fig tree by the road “and found nothing at all on it but leaves.” He says: “May no fruit ever come from you again!” and the tree withers. This is one of the few miracles of judgement in the Gospels, and it is a parable acted out. The prophets had used the fig tree as an image of God's people: “there are no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree” (Jeremiah 8:13). A tree covered in leaves promises fruit from far away; up close it has nothing to give. Leaves without fruit are what James calls hearing without doing. Jesus does not stop at the warning. When the disciples marvel, he turns the moment into a lesson on prayer: “Truly I tell you, if you have faith and do not doubt, not only will you do what has been done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and thrown into the sea,’ it will be done. Whatever you ask for in prayer with faith, you will receive.” The power that can wither a fruitless tree is the same power that can make a dry tree bear fruit. The Risen Lord does not want us to wither; he wants us to pray with faith and bear the fruit of the grace already given to us in Baptism and in the Holy Qurbana. In April and May many parishes run their vacation Bible classes, and children learn the words of Scripture by heart. The best lesson they can receive is to see their parents doing those words.
outline: Opening
A metal mirror from Aranmula: do I forget my face as soon as I walk away?
Point 1 · Doers, not only hearers
The mirror of the word.
Point 2 · Religion pure and undefiled
The bridled tongue, the orphan and the widow.
Point 3 · Leaves without fruit
The fig tree, and prayer that moves mountains.
Take-home line
“Be doers of the word, and not merely hearers.”
live: Do one word (James 1:22)
Choose one sentence from last Sunday's Gospel and put it into practice before Sunday comes again.
Visit the orphan and the widow (James 1:27)
This week, visit or call one widow, one elderly person living alone, or one home for children, and bring something with you.
fathers: St Gregory the Great (in substance)
The proof of love is the showing of the deed. The love of God is never idle: where it is present it does great things; where it refuses to work, it is not love.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Do you wish to honour the body of Christ? Do not neglect him when he is naked. Do not honour him here in the church with silk vestments and then pass him by outside, where he is cold and without clothing. What use is it to load his table with golden cups when he himself is dying of hunger?
magis: Catechism 2447

The works of mercy are charitable actions by which we come to the help of our neighbour in his bodily and spiritual needs: feeding the hungry, sheltering the homeless, visiting the sick and the imprisoned.
Catechism 2610
Jesus teaches the filial boldness of faith in prayer: whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it.
Catechism 1815
Faith without works is dead: when it is deprived of hope and love, faith does not fully unite the believer to Christ.
2027-04-27.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen and living, you came to the fig tree hungry and found only leaves. Do not find our lives full of words and empty of fruit. Make us doers of your word and not hearers only; bridle our tongues, open our hands to the orphan and the widow, and keep us unstained by the world. Give us faith that does not doubt, so that we may pray with boldness and bear the fruit of your grace. Amen. Alleluia!
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the word we hear becomes the Body we receive. The Lord who feeds us at the altar sends us out to feed the hungry, so that our thanksgiving may bear fruit in the street.

2027-04-28.title: Fifth Wednesday of Resurrection
2027-04-28.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Born again of water and the Spirit
2027-04-28.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost.
2027-04-28.verse: Very truly, I tell you, no one can enter the kingdom of God without being born of water and Spirit.
theo: Nicodemus comes to Jesus by night. He is a Pharisee, “a leader of the Jews”, a teacher of Israel, a man of learning and position, and he comes with respect: “Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher who has come from God; for no one can do these signs that you do apart from the presence of God.” Jesus does not answer the compliment. He goes straight to the deepest need: “Very truly, I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God without being born from above.” The Greek word means both ‘again’ and ‘from above’, and Nicodemus hears only the first meaning: “How can anyone be born after having grown old? Can one enter a second time into the mother's womb and be born?” His question is honest, even a little humorous. He is perhaps no longer young, and he knows he cannot start his life again. Jesus answers that this is exactly what God offers: not a second birth from a human mother, but a new birth from God. “Very truly, I tell you, no one can enter the kingdom of God without being born of water and Spirit. What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit.” The Church has always heard in these words the sacrament of Baptism. In the East Syriac tradition the baptismal font is spoken of as a womb, from which the Church our mother gives birth to children of God.

Jesus adds an image that only makes sense in the open air: “The wind blows where it chooses, and you hear the sound of it, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.” In Aramaic, as in Greek, one word means both wind and spirit: ruha. Anyone who has stood on a Kerala beach before the monsoon knows the wind that cannot be seen but bends every coconut palm. The Spirit given in Baptism works like that, unseen but not unfelt. Nicodemus leaves the scene still puzzled, but John does not forget him. Later he speaks up for Jesus before the council (John 7:50–51), and after the Crucifixion he comes, no longer by night, carrying a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes to bury the body of the Lord (John 19:39). The man who asked how one who had grown old could be born again found his answer at the foot of the Cross and beside the tomb that was soon to be empty. New birth is not always sudden; it can be a slow walk from night into day. In these weeks many of our parishes celebrate the First Holy Communion of children, who were born of water and Spirit as infants and now come to the altar for the first time. It is a good moment for every adult in the church to ask whether the life begun in their own Baptism is still growing.

Paul tells the Colossians what that new life looks like in practice. Since you have been raised with Christ, he says, there are things that must die: “Put to death, therefore, whatever in you is earthly: fornication, impurity, passion, evil desire, and greed (which is idolatry).” Then the sins of the mouth: “But now you must get rid of all such things: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and abusive language from your mouth. Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have stripped off the old self with its practices and have clothed yourselves with the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge according to the image of its creator.” The image is of a garment.
